articles.title: VP Sara's defense team no longer presenting BPI official
articles.summary: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday decided not to present a witness from Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) for her impeachment trial.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 11:25am
The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday decided not to present a witness from Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) for her impeachment trial.

Defense counsel Michael Poa said Atty. Paul Roderick Ysmael, senior vice president of the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), won’t stand as a defense witness anymore because it was already established that Poa wrote a letter to the BPI about the bank accounts of the Vice President and her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte.

“The reason being that the only purpose for this witness was to authenticate my letter, Your Honor, and I believe the records would bear that during interpellation, I was already asked about the letter, and I have admitted in open court that I wrote that letter,” Poa told the Senate impeachment court.

Ysmael was supposed to bring and identify certified true copies of the letter-requests of the Vice President and/or her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio, through counsel Poa, Himala and Virtucio Law, in 2026.

“It would be in the interest of time that we just dispensed with this witness, since this is only for the purpose of authentication. And that letter of mine has already been marked as well as an exhibit for the defense,” Poa added.

Prosecution witness Marwin Galvez, division head for central Manila branches of BPI, earlier testified that a joint bank account under the name of Vice President and her father was used to purchase a P16-million manager's check for businessman Sammy Uy.
Prosecution's response

Private prosecutor James Ali responded by asking the Senate impeachment court if the prosecution can put forward manifestations on documents that were subpoenaed by the court for the testimony of BPI official Ysmael.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, however, denied Ali’s request given that the prosecution had already rested its case.
The defense earlier dropped 15 bank official witnesses, saying it was "in the interest of time." —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Witnesses' unsatisfactory answers not contemptible -- Escudero
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said Thursday that answers of witnesses that are deemed unsatisfactory by senator-judges do not constitute grounds for contempt.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 11:16am
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said Thursday that answers of witnesses that are deemed unsatisfactory by senator-judges do not constitute grounds for contempt.

Escudero said this on the 43rd day of the impeachment trial, stressing that all witnesses are entitled to the rights listed under Rule 132, Section 3, of the Rules on Evidence, which have suppletory application to the proceedings, even as they took an oath before the court to testify truthfully and to answer all questions.

“The Chair wishes to emphasize that an answer which may be unsatisfactory is not inherently contemptible. Supreme Court cases have cautioned courts to use the power of contempt with the highest restraint,” the presiding officer said.
Escudero likewise reminded the members of the court, including himself, who earlier said that his patience was “wearing thin,” that they are sitting as senator-judges in a trial.
“Our rules behoove us to receive and evaluate the evidence with impartiality and, due to the often lengthy examination by both parties, with utmost patience as well,” he added.

On Tuesday, senator-judges called out Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan, a witness fielded by the defense, for supposedly being evasive and taking a long time to respond to questions being asked during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Escudero back then said that his patience was “wearing thin,” considering the repeated answers of the witness that she could not remember details or is not familiar with documents presented by private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia.

The presiding officer also reminded the counsels for both parties, as well as senator-judges, that while they may rigorously examine witnesses and test the credibility of their testimonies, they “must refrain from resorting to a manner of questioning or to making declarations that elicit fear rather than candor.”
“The Chair therefore respectfully requests our distinguished colleagues, the counsels for the parties, including this representation, to exercise the restraint expected of us,” he said.

“Unlike in inquiries in aid of legislation, an answer of ‘I do not know’ or ‘I do not recall’ may be extremely frustrating. It’s one that we may encounter numerous times in a proceeding such as this. What we can control, however, is how we appreciate and weigh the testimonies and statements delivered before this Court,” he added.

Escudero said that they owe it to the parties, witnesses, and the institution they represent to conduct the proceedings with fairness, dignity and respect, “in spite and despite our frustration and/or disappointment with what the witness may or may not be saying.” — RSJ, GMA News

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 11:16am
The Philippines is not picking fights with China but is standing its ground in defending its rights in the West Philippine Sea (WPS), Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. said.
In an ambush interview on Wednesday, Teodoro was asked about Vice President Sara Duterte's statement that the country should avoid picking fights considering China’s military strength.
“Unang-una, and most importantly, hindi naman tayo nakikipag-away pero naninindigan naman tayo,” Teodoro said.
(First and foremost, and most importantly, we are not fighting but we are standing our ground.)

“I mean, the disparity of size is also a consideration pero kung pinaglalaban natin ay batas at kinabukasan ng ating mga susunod na henerasyon, I think there's no compromise. And I'll stop there. I think the Filipinos know that it is a false choice,” he added.

(I mean, the disparity in size is also a consideration but if what we are fighting for is the law and the future of our future generations, I think there's no compromise. And I'll stop there. I think the Filipinos know that it is a false choice.)
Speaking at a gathering with Filipino workers in Hong Kong on Sunday, Duterte suggested that resolving issues is better handled through diplomatic talks rather than heated exchanges online.

“Alam ninyo dapat kasi hindi nakikipag-away ang gobyerno o ang opsiyal ng gobyerno sa kahit na anong bansa dahil napaka-complicated ng relasyon ng dalawang bansa. Hindi lang siya isang bagay lang, maraming aspeto ang relasyon ng Pilipinas sa bawat bansa,” Duterte said.

(The government or a government official should not pick a fight with any country because bilateral relations are very complicated. It is not just a single matter; there are many aspects to the Philippines' relationship with every nation.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: ASEAN Summit: Metro Manila road closures, alternate routes, traffic advisories
articles.summary: (Updated) What commuters and travelers need to know for ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 11:10am

MANILA, Philippines (Updated Nov. 12; First published Oct. 29, 2026.) — Motorists, commuters and air travelers should prepare for road closures, traffic restrictions and possible flight disruptions as Metro Manila hosts the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in November.
The summit will run from Nov. 16 to 18 at several venues across the capital, primarily the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City.
Security preparations will affect road access around the venue and may also lead to changes in airport operations.
Special non-working days: Nov. 16 to 18

Malacañang has declared Nov. 16 to 18 special non-working days throughout Metro Manila. This is when the ASEAN Leaders Summit will take place. U.S. President Donald Trump is among the leaders expected to attend the meetings.
Under Proclamation 1447, the work suspension is intended to ease traffic congestion and allow authorities to secure areas used by summit participants.
Road restrictions

The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority explained on Wednesday, November 11, that there will be no widespread road closures during the summit, with restrictions limited to designated security zones around the Philippine International Convention Center and Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex in Pasay City.
However, motorists should prepare for temporary traffic stoppages along major thoroughfares whenever convoys carrying foreign leaders and delegations pass through.

MMDA Chairman Romando Artes warned that traffic could be particularly heavy from November 12 to 14 because of convoy rehearsals, traffic simulations, road repairs and adjustments to barriers ahead of the summit.
Access to four streets within the PICC and CCP security exclusion zone is restricted from November 9 to 18, according to the MMDA.
These are:

items: Atang Dela Rama Street
Vicente Sotto Street
Pedro Bukaneg Street
Magdalena Jalandoni Street

blocks.text: Only accredited personnel and vehicles bearing authorized ASEAN stickers will be allowed inside the restricted perimeter. Government vehicles without proper authorization will also be denied entry.
The MMDA said other major roads will remain open, although motorists should expect delays and temporary traffic restrictions during the movement of official convoys.
Authorities have also advised motorists to avoid Macapagal Boulevard, the World Trade Center area, Diokno Boulevard and portions of Roxas Boulevard because of anticipated traffic congestion.
The MMDA said access restrictions around the PICC will be implemented in two phases.
MMDA
Alternate routes and traffic adjustments
The MMDA has designated alternate routes for vehicles traveling near the PICC and CCP Complex.
Southbound motorists traveling along Roxas Boulevard toward Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard may take the following route:

items: Turn right onto EDSA.
Turn right onto Diokno Boulevard.
Turn right onto Macapagal Boulevard.

blocks.text: Northbound motorists traveling along Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard toward Roxas Boulevard may take:

items: Turn right onto Seaside Boulevard.
Turn right onto Macapagal Boulevard.
Turn left onto EDSA.
Turn left onto Roxas Boulevard.

blocks.text: The MMDA will also implement a stop-and-go traffic scheme along roads used by official convoys. Traffic will be temporarily halted when heads of state and their delegations pass, then allowed to resume afterward.
Artes said these interruptions would generally last only a few minutes.
Truck operators will also be required to follow designated routes from Nov. 15 to 18 to keep container trucks away from Roxas Boulevard.
The alternative truck routes cover roads connecting Manila's Port Area, North Harbor, North Diversion Road and President Osmeña Highway.
EDSA bus lanes, number coding
Designated EDSA bus lanes will be shared with official summit convoys to facilitate the movement of foreign delegates.

The Department of Transportation said buses will continue using the lanes, while traffic personnel will manage their movement to accommodate diplomatic convoys. Private motorists may continue using the regular EDSA lanes.
Motorists approaching the Magallanes Flyover from the Ayala Tunnel should also expect temporary traffic stoppages.
Meanwhile, the MMDA has suspended the number coding scheme from Monday, November 16, to Wednesday, November 18.
The MMDA said it will deploy 2,637 personnel to assist with traffic management and security operations, including emergency response teams and towing personnel.
Motorists and commuters are advised to allow additional travel time, follow posted traffic instructions and monitor official MMDA advisories for further adjustments.

articles.title: Historic US ocean liner sinks near Florida to become world’s largest artificial reef
articles.summary:
SS United States, which set transatlantic speed record during maiden voyage in 1952, is sunk off coast of Destin

The historic SS United States has reached the end of its journey at sea,…

blocks.text: The historic SS United States has reached the end of its journey at sea, sinking Wednesday off the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will begin a new life underwater as an artificial reef.

The nearly 1,000ft American-made vessel, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, was launched in 1952 and made history by setting a transatlantic speed record during its maiden voyage. The ship carried thousands of passengers across the Atlantic over 17 years of operation before being retired in 1969.

On Wednesday, the ship was deployed at approximately 2.40pm ET, with the sinking process beginning shortly before 5pm. The ship had been hollowed out, with openings cut into its hull to let water in and help it sink upright to the ocean floor. Over the next several hours, the ship gradually filled with water before finally sinking to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico around 10pm.

It will rest on the seafloor at a depth of approximately 180ft, the ship’s upper decks sitting about 55ft below the surface. As the world’s largest artificial reef, the site is expected to become a popular diving destination for divers around the world.

For years, the SS United States remained docked in Philadelphia, as various owners attempted to save and restore it. However, the rising costs of maintaining the ageing vessel complicated preservation efforts. In 2021, port authorities raised the daily dockage fee to $1,700, a cost the non-profit SS United States Conservancy could no longer afford.

In 2024, Florida’s Okaloosa county purchased the ship for $1m, with plans to transform it into the world’s largest artificial reef. Officials expect the structure to provide a new habitat for a variety of marine life, including red snapper, grouper, amberjack, mackerel and tuna.

Before its sinking, Susan Gibbs, president and co-founder of the conservancy, said: “She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat, so that, combined with the land-based museum and visitor experience, will honor her history in a deeply moving way.”

Gibbs, whose grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the ship, also reflected on his personal connection to the vessel, saying: “His relationship with the ship was, I would say, a full-bore obsession. He would joke that he loved the SS United States a thousand times more than my grandmother. He would see the ship off every time she set sail for Europe, and be one of the first to greet her on her return.”

articles.title: Philippines faces difficult mix of high inflation, sluggish growth — BSP
articles.summary: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is focusing on the “second-round effects” of global supply shocks and the risk of eroding public trust as the country faces “a difficult…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 11:07am
Fresh vegetables are displayed at a market in Quezon City on March 4, 2026.
Michael Varcas / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is focusing on the “second-round effects” of global supply shocks and the risk of eroding public trust as the country faces “a difficult combination” of rising inflation and sluggish growth.

The BSP said on Wednesday, November 12, that it is also considering weak aggregate demand as it works to bring inflation down. It added that restoring price stability and purchasing power is crucial to rebuilding public confidence in the central bank and the economy.

"Signs of improvement would include easing inflation, more stable inflation expectations, stronger business and consumer confidence, and a recovery in investment and employment," the central bank said.

Intending to bring inflation back to its 3% target by 2028, the BSP has raised its benchmark interest rate by 125 basis points in 2026 alone, with a "jumbo" 50-basis-point hike implemented in October.
Inflation for the same month was recorded at a three-year high of 7.8%, driven by high energy and transport costs. Economic growth, meanwhile, weakened to 2.1% in the third quarter of 2026.
The BSP will convene for its final Monetary Board meeting on December 17 and release its last monetary policy report on December 23.

articles.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.summary:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from…

blocks.text: The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.

blocks.caption: Before and after satellite images of an oil spill off the coast of UAE in October

blocks.text: Ecosystem at risk

The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.

It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.

blocks.caption: Oil washes up on a beach in Umm Al Quwain, UAE, on 24 October. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.

Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.

“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.

“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Strikes and spills

Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.

“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.

More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.

Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.

blocks.caption: The Gem No 2 ablaze at sea

blocks.text: Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.

blocks.caption: The Minoan Pioneer off the coast of Muscat, Oman, on 30 October. Photograph: Arnel Hecimovic/The Guardian

blocks.text: Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Before and after images of an oil slick off UAE in October

blocks.text: Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.

blocks.caption: A satellite image showing an oil slick spreading off the coast of Kharg Island, a key oil export terminal for Iran, in May. Photograph: Copernicus Sentinel data/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.

Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.
The damage ahead

In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman, divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.

blocks.caption: An oil slick along the southern coast of Qeshm Island, Iran, on 13 August. Photograph: ISNA/AFP/Getty Images
Beaches being closed in UAE after oil spills caused by tanker attacks

blocks.text: But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.

Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”

Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.

A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.

blocks.caption: Workers clean a stretch of beach after oil washed ashore in Sharjah, UAE, 3 November. Photograph: Altaf Qadri/AP

blocks.text: Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title: When Indigenous Peoples survive, the rest of us do too
articles.summary: We cannot control when El Niño arrives, but we can control how much of our natural defense — forests, watersheds, water, rivers — we destroy before it does

blocks.text: Across the country, Indigenous Peoples have been sounding a warning we have been slow to hear.

“Ang proyektong iyan ay isang dambuhalang linta na sisipsipin lahat ng yaman ng bundok. Hindi naman po pansarili ang aming ipinaglalaban.” (That project is a giant leech that will suck the mountain dry of its riches. What we are fighting for is not for ourselves alone.)
These were the words of an Aeta elder opposing the proposed Pax Silica development in Tarlac.
Farther south, in General Nakar, Quezon, a Dumagat mother who marched 150 kilometers to oppose the Kaliwa Dam, spoke of the burden she carried:

“Tuwing naglalakad po kami, tuwing naiisip ko ang gagawin sa amin at mangyayari sa amin at sa susunod na henerasyon, halos ako po ay naiiyak sa daan dahil pakiramdam ko pasan ko ang Sierra Madre.” (Every time we walk, when I think about what will happen to us and to the generations after us, I almost cry because I feel as though I am carrying the Sierra Madre on my shoulders.)
Communities and environmental groups warn that the dam threatens the biodiversity of the Sierra Madre.

A giant leech draining a mountain. A Dumagat mother carrying the Sierra Madre on her shoulders. Different communities, different threats, but the same warning: what is being lost in the name of progress does not belong to them alone.

The Philippines is once again confronting El Niño, with warnings of drought, threats to food security, and pressure on our water supply. While we ask how to withstand a hotter, drier future, people long pushed aside in the name of progress have practiced resilience for generations. They remind us that survival depends not only on what we take from the Earth, but on what we leave behind.

There is a small pouch I have never forgotten. Some time ago, while spending time with an Indigenous community, I noticed that a fisherman carried a pouch barely larger than a clutch bag. I asked why he did not bring something bigger. “That is enough for one day,” he answered. “Tomorrow is another day. The river provides what is needed. To take more is to take from someone else.” In that tiny pouch lived a philosophy deeper than many policy papers: enough is enough.

Yet as we are told to conserve water and become more resilient to climate change, we continue to place ancestral lands and ecosystems in the path of development. Healthy forests and watersheds regulate water, sustain rivers, and help shield us from drought, floods, and extreme heat. We cannot control when El Niño arrives, but we can control how much of our natural defense we destroy before it does. Preparedness begins long before reservoirs fall and crops wither. It begins with what we choose to protect.

Consider Capas, Tarlac. The proposed Pax Silica technology hub promises artificial intelligence infrastructure, semiconductor development, investment, and jobs. But Aeta communities fear displacement and threats to ancestral lands, livelihoods, and water sources.

The collision is almost too symbolic: a people rooted in the land for generations confronting an industry meant to carry us into the technological future. Beneath it lies an older question: What is land worth?

To most of us, land is property, with titles, market values, and development potential. To many Indigenous Peoples, it is something else entirely. I have met various Indigenous groups with different cultures and traditions, yet when they speak of land, I hear the same truth: Ang lupa ay buhay.
The land is life. It is where ancestors are buried and children are born. Rivers hold stories. Mountains mark histories. Forests are pharmacies, kitchens, classrooms, and places of worship.

I have seen what that relationship looks like through my work with Bantay Gubat rangers, many of whom are Dumagat. These forest guardians patrol the Ipo Watershed, confronting illegal logging, illegal settlement, forest fires, and other threats. They risk their lives protecting a watershed that helps provide water to millions in Metro Manila.
There, the connection between their survival and ours becomes tangible: in protecting their ancestral forests, they are also protecting the water that flows into our homes.

And they are hardly alone. On Sibuyan Island in Romblon, often called the “Galápagos of Asia” for its extraordinary biodiversity, the Sibuyan Mangyan Tagabukid, alongside fellow Sibuyanons and environmental advocates, have resisted nickel mining they fear threatens the island’s ecosystems. In 2023, residents formed a human barricade against trucks carrying nickel ore, putting their bodies in the path of mining operations to protect the island they call home.

In Boracay, behind the powdery white sand and postcard-perfect resorts lies another story: the Ati have faced displacement and the loss of traditional livelihoods as tourism and development transformed their ancestral lands.

In Bugsuk, Palawan, Molbog and Pala’wan communities have fought for ancestral lands and fishing waters threatened by private commercial interests, including pearl farming — a struggle Indigenous advocates call “blood pearls.”

In Kalinga, the historic resistance of the Kalinga and Bontok peoples to the Chico River Dam lives on, as members of the Balatoc community resist mining and communities along the Chico River raise concerns over hydropower projects threatening their ancestral lands and livelihoods.
The project changes — a technology hub, a dam, a mine, a resort. The generation changes. The landscape changes. But the question remains: Who gets to decide what Indigenous land and water are worth?

Progress need not come at the expense of preservation. We can build economies that restore rather than exhaust, create livelihoods that sustain rather than displace, and pursue development that strengthens our resilience rather than deepens our vulnerabilities. The measure of progress should be not only what we gain, but what we preserve for generations to come.

The answer matters far beyond these communities. An estimated 85% of the Philippines’ Key Biodiversity Areas lie within ancestral domains. Yet Indigenous Peoples continue to face threats from mining, quarrying, logging, land conversion, infrastructure, and even poorly planned renewable energy projects.

Too often, we reduce the living world to what it can produce: a forest becomes timber, a mountain becomes minerals, a river becomes cubic meters of water, a coastline becomes real estate. But not everything of value can be priced. In safeguarding the land, we safeguard ourselves.

Their rights need no justification beyond the fact that they are rights. But there is another truth we can no longer ignore: their survival is bound to our own. Their struggles may unfold far from our homes, yet the fate of those places does not end at the borders of ancestral lands. What they protect sustains us. What they lose, we eventually lose too.
So perhaps honoring Indigenous Peoples should begin with something harder: listening — to both the cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor, as Laudato Si’ urges us.
Ang lupa ay buhay. The land is life. And, without it, none of us survives. – Rappler.com

Sarah Bautista-Abaño is an environmental and human rights advocate who has worked closely with Indigenous communities on ancestral land rights, environmental protection, and community empowerment. A trained wildlife ranger, she has served alongside Indigenous forest guardians protecting critical watersheds and forests. She is also a wife, mother of three daughters, and avid mountaineer.

articles.title: Prosecution: Comparison of P2M GenCorp income of VP Sara to Cabrera report 'misplaced'
articles.summary: The defense team comparing GenCorp. Industries. Inc."s P2.14 million payout to Vice President Sara Duterte based on the said company"s books to the alleged P212 million undeclared income of the Vice…

blocks.text: The defense team comparing GenCorp. Industries. Inc.’s P2.14 million payout to Vice President Sara Duterte based on the company’s books to the alleged P212 million undeclared income of the Vice President from GenCorp. Industries based on analysis of multiple financial records by Atty. Alex Cabrera is a misplaced comparison, the House prosecution team said.

House prosecutor Rodge Gutierrez and private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr. were referring to the testimony by GenCorp.’s in-house legal counsel, Suzette Punay, during Day 42 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President.

Punay testified that GenCorp. disbursed P2.14 million return of capital payout to the Vice President due to her loose investment in the firm based on corporate records from 2022 to 2025. Punay, however, said that she is not aware of any document showing as to why the Vice President was paid such amount even if the Vice President’s investment was made to a different firm that was supposed to operate a Jollibee branch that did not push through.

“It is very clear that what has been established by the defense is not the complete picture, and this has been backed up by the questioning of some of the Senator judges. She has limited personal knowledge on the matter, and that is the thing the judges would have to consider about that P2 milion,” Gutierrez said in a press conference after Day 42 of the trial.

“I think it's comparing an apple seed to the apple because she only saw a small portion of GenCorp. records. On the other hand, Atty. Cabrera has seen the bank records, corporate records and the Vice President’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth. He considered everything. So that’s the proper analogy if we’re going to give one,” Gutierrez added.
Tolosa agreed as Punay herself admitted that she has not conducted a forensic audit before as compared with Cabrera, who was qualified by the Senate impeachment court as an "expert witness."

Likewise, Tolosa said it is suspect that Punay was categorical in saying that the P2 million GenCorp. disbursement to the Vice President has basis even if she did not see any document why GenCorp. Is making such payout to the Vice President when the latter invested in another firm.

“The P2 million was based on a loose investments which was not able to prove with any documentary basis [as to why GenCorp. Made such payout]. And she can't even say what are the terms of this supposed contract [justifying GenCorp’s payout when the Vice President invested in another firm],” Tolosa said.

“She believes this loose investment even if she didn't see any document. But on the other hand, she's saying, I can't believe the computation of Atty. Cabrera because she has not seen the [pertinent] documents. I mean, if you'll go by your theory that you can believe the investment even if you don't see any document, why can't you believe a Atty. Cabrera?,” Tolosa added.

The defense is presenting its evidence against Article 2 which accuses the Vice President of betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution due to amassing P817 million to P1.5 billion of unexplained wealth due to non-declaration of assets and non-divestment in businesses despite a Constitutional ban. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
articles.summary: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".

blocks.text: A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Friday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

articles.title: Australian teen who went missing in bushland wearing only shorts and boots found alive after six days
articles.summary:
William, 17, was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla in Victoria’s Gippsland region

  • Get our

blocks.text: A teenage boy has been found alive after disappearing in dense bushland wearing only shorts and work boots nearly a week ago.
Police AirWing found William, 17, whose surname has not been shared, on Thursday morning.
The teenager was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla, 185km east of Melbourne, in Victoria’s Gippsland region last Friday.
He was dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend.
It is believed he walked a short distance back to the drop-off location to retrieve further camping equipment.
When he failed to return shortly after, his stepbrother searched the area but found no trace of the teen.
William’s mobile phone, food and water were left behind.
Police said he was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, between Cowwarr and Walhalla on 6 November about 4pm.
On Wednesday, investigators appealed to hunters, campers and landowners to come forward with any information after a hunting camera was found in the search area.
Emergency service workers, including the dog and rescue squad had been searching the dense bushland since last Friday.

articles.summary: Jensen Huang's potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4-trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades

Jensen Huang's potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4-trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades

items: Nvidia's board is meeting to discuss the potential ousting of CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, which has led to a significant drop in the company's stock value.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and has maintained tight control over the company, currently has no clear successor, raising concerns about leadership stability.

The controversy surrounding Huang includes investigations into his relationships and potential foreign intelligence involvement, with implications for Nvidia's market position and investor confidence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Nvidia’s board is meeting on Wednesday, November 11, to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors grapples with reports of two extramarital affairs involving its longtime leader.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the board meeting.

Huang’s potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4-trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of AI chips at the center of the global artificial-intelligence boom and US-China technology rivalry.
Huang, 63, has no obvious successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. He also has dozens of direct reports, underscoring the tight control he maintains over the company.

“Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place … If Mr. Huang broke the law or violated company policies, the board is likely to act as soon as they have proof,” Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said.

The company’s shares slid about 8% in after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal first reported that Nvidia was preparing to oust Huang. Including Wednesday’s after-hours selloff, Nvidia has lost about $600 billion in stock market value this week since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman.
Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.
The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five people who worked at the company.
When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up, the New York Times reported.
Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.

The reports mark a sharp escalation in a controversy that began with revelations about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence has said was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

US stock futures sank, with Nasdaq futures down 1%. However, shares of rival chipmakers AMD and Broadcom rose 4% and 3%, respectively, in after-hours trading, which an analyst said reflected the view that those chip producers would pick up market share.
Investors and analysts said while demand for Nvidia’s chips would be unlikely to drop in the near term, the broader universe of companies backed by the company might suffer.
“Nvidia is also at the center of the circular financing which is providing capital to the investment boom,” said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management in Singapore.
“They are financing their customers. In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase.”
In a memo to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and took “full responsibility,” but gave no details about the relationship.

The same day, Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The probe is being overseen by independent directors with outside legal counsel. At the time, the board expressed confidence in Huang.

US President Donald Trump has said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang but voiced support for the Nvidia chief, calling him “an honorable guy” who had “done an amazing job for our country.”

Huang faces a potential congressional subpoena if he doesn’t respond to a request to provide a closed-door briefing about the allegations that he had a close relationship with the Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

Separately, Axios reported on Wednesday, citing high-level sources, that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Donald Trump’s crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s chips to China.

blocks.caption: Trump’s close ties to Nvidia’s Huang scrutinized after foreign intelligence concerns

blocks.text: The White House and a spokesperson for Lutnick did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with Curtis Priem and Chris Malachowsky. Its early hits were graphics chips for computer games, before its CUDA software opened the processors to general computing and, later, AI. – Rappler.com

articles.title: PH standing up for rights in WPS, not looking for fight – DND chief
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. clarified that the country is not picking fights or seeking confrontation when it stands up for its rights in the West Philippine Sea…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. clarified that the country is not picking fights or seeking confrontation when it stands up for its rights in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

“Unang una, and most importantly, hindi naman tayo nakikipag-away eh, pero naninindigan naman tayo (First of all, and most importantly, we are not looking for a fight, but we are only making a stand),” he said in a chance interview with reporters in Cebu City on Wednesday.
Teodoro was responding to comments that the Philippines should not confront China over its claims in the WPS because of the vast differences in their respective militaries’ strength and size.

“Pero kung pinaglalaban natin ay batas at ang kinabukasan ng ating mga susunod na henerasyon (But if we are fighting for the rule of law and the future of the next generation), I think there’s no compromise,” he said.

Earlier, retired Navy reservist Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) spokesperson for the WPS, clarified that Philippine officials are not picking fights with China even as they strive to protect the country’s sovereignty in the vital waterway.

“Hindi po tayo nakikipag-away sa kahit sino mang bansa sa WPS. Tayo lamang ay tumatayo sa ating karapatan na pinagkaloob ng Diyos sa atin, yung ating maritime entitlements, yung ating sovereignty and sovereign rights (we are not picking fights with any country regarding the WPS. We are just standing up for our God-given rights, our maritime entitlements, our sovereignty and sovereign rights),” he said.
Trinidad was referring to calls from some sectors asking the country to tone down its stance on the issue.
“We are not fighting any other country. Ito ay tinatayuan natin sapagkat ito ay mandato ng inyong DND and AFP (we are standing up for this because this is the mandate of the DND and AFP),” he said.
He also said they want the next generation of Filipinos to inherit a whole and free country.
“And all those maritime entitlements within the EEZ (exclusive economic zone) will be for them to benefit,” Trinidad said. /jpv

articles.title: Indonesia’s vice president has resigned, aide says, stoking political uncertainty
articles.summary: Gibran, son of ex-president Joko Widodo, has come under intense scrutiny from lawmakers following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings that his education documents did not meet election…

blocks.text: VEEP. Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka attends the inauguration of newly appointed Head of the National Nutrition Agency and special advisor for manpower and labour welfare affairs, at the State Palace in Jakarta, Indonesia, June 8, 2026. REUTERS
Willy Kurniawan/REUTERS

Gibran, son of ex-president Joko Widodo, has come under intense scrutiny from lawmakers following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings that his education documents did not meet election requirements

items: Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned amid scrutiny over his education credentials, threatening a key political alliance.
His resignation follows a Supreme Court ruling that his education documents do not meet election requirements, leading to calls for impeachment from lawmakers.
The political instability could further weaken investor sentiment towards Indonesia, which is already facing challenges related to its fiscal plans and governance.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

JAKARTA, Indonesia – Indonesia‘s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned, an aide said on Wednesday, November 11, a move that threatens to split a key political alliance and risks further political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.

Gibran, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, has come under intense scrutiny from lawmakers following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings last month that his education documents did not meet election requirements.
The aide, Budi Arie Setiadi, told Reuters that Gibran had tendered his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto earlier on Wednesday.

Separately, two sources at the parliamentary upper house, which will oversee the process of approving his resignation and selecting a replacement, said that he would submit his resignation letter to the upper house on Thursday morning.
Neither Gibran’s office nor Prabowo’s office immediately responded to a request for comment.
Late on Wednesday, Prabowo gave a long speech at a political party event. He did not mention Gibran’s resignation.

The resignation comes amid growing signs of strain in the political alliance between Prabowo, a powerful former general, and Widodo, also known as Jokowi, a highly popular leader who twice defeated Prabowo for the presidency before giving him his support after facing term limits.

An open split could spark further instability for an administration hit by scandals over signature programmes, such as its free school meals policy, and doubts over its handling of the economy, political analysts say.

Investor sentiment has weakened towards Indonesia this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government’s fiscal plans and its broader policy directions, as well as lingering downgrade risks for its stock market by global index provider MSCI.
Last week, Prabowo fired his chief of staff, widely seen as a Jokowi loyalist, after he was arrested on accusations of bugging the president, among other figures.
Gibran stated his intention to resign during a meeting with Prabowo on Tuesday.

The parliamentary upper house will have to convene a session to declare a vacancy following the submission of Gibran’s resignation letter, while writing a letter to the president requesting that he submit two names for his replacement, said senior law minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra.
After that, the upper house would hold an election within 60 days.
Earlier on Wednesday, some 120 Indonesian lawmakers from across the political spectrum submitted a petition demanding Gibran’s impeachment, fuelling tensions around his political future.
Gibran “no longer meets the requirements as vice president as stipulated in Indonesia’s constitution,” said Mardani Ali Sera, one of the lawmakers who signed the petition.

Gibran faced complaints over whether his education credentials met legal requirements, and on Tuesday the Supreme Court said it was instructing the education ministry to withdraw Gibran’s education equivalence certificate, which the court has annulled.
Gibran, who studied abroad, used the certificate to comply with education requirements and run in the 2024 election, which he won alongside Prabowo.

Indonesian election law requires vice-presidential candidates to have completed senior high ​school or an equivalent level of education, but the court found that the certificate was issued based on evidence that did not actually prove Jokowi’s eldest son had graduated.

“No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification,” the court said in the ruling.
The Supreme Court also took into account the Constitutional Court’s ruling, which said Gibran’s education documents did not meet election requirements.

Gibran’s spot on the 2024 ticket was previously marred by ethics complaints after the Constitutional Court, headed at the time by his uncle, removed an age limit that would have prevented his candidacy.

Sana Jaffrey, a ⁠researcher at the Australian National University, said the crisis showed how the political fortunes of a small number of elites took precedence over the country’s need for effective and stable governance.
“Prolonged uncertainty at the highest levels of power will only deepen anxieties at home and abroad about where the country is headed,” she said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Hegseth, wife and aides spark scolding from guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a…

image.caption: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, his wife, Jennifer, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine attend a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., on Wednesday. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony.
Pentagon spokesman said U.S. army sentinel 'correctly and respectfully' called for proper decorum
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured — and will always honour — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.
Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
Incident follows near impeachment of Hegseth

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth slammed the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.
Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.
"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.
"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post.

Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office. One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.—RepGwenMoore
It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honour U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.
U.S. army confirms Arlington cemetery worker 'pushed aside' by Trump staff

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

articles.title: PNP braces for expected long weekend rush amid ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) has intensified its security and public safety operations nationwide in light of the expected influx of travelers during the long weekend in Metro Manila amid the…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 9:06am

The Philippine National Police (PNP) has intensified its security and public safety operations nationwide in light of the expected influx of travelers during the long weekend in Metro Manila amid the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

“Our commanders down to the station level were already tasked to strengthen police visibility and intensify patrol operations in major transport hubs, seaports, airports, bus terminals, highways, and tourist destinations,” PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement.
“We want every Filipino to enjoy the long weekend with the assurance that the PNP is present, prepared, and ready to respond to any security concern,” he added.

Authorities expect more Filipinos to travel to their hometowns and vacation destinations starting this weekend after Malacañang declared November 16 to 18 as special non-working days for ASEAN Summit 2026.
The expected influx of travelers comes after authorities recorded a decline in passengers at various ports during the observance of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day.

“They attributed the decrease to a short holiday and expressed belief that more Filipinos would choose to travel to their hometowns and other vacation sites starting this weekend due to the longer holiday break,” PNP said.
Meanwhile, government agencies have activated emergency response contingents for the ASEAN Summit.

The contingents consist of 774 personnel and 119 specialized assets, including ambulances, fire trucks, engineering equipment, transport vehicles, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) units, tactical communications equipment, and Starlink satellite systems, according to PNP.

Nartatez reminded travelers to take precautions before leaving their homes, follow traffic and travel regulations, remain vigilant against criminal activities, and report suspicious incidents to the nearest police unit.
“We encourage everyone to make the most of the long weekend but never at the expense of safety and responsibility,” Nartatez said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Australian states could sue tobacco companies for billions in healthcare costs under proposal
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Former barrister who helped legally establish that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer argues states could seek up to $50bn in compensation

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australian state governments could sue tobacco companies for billions in public hospital and healthcare costs, under a proposal developed by a former barrister who helped legally establish that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer.
The South Australian government is formally seeking advice on the proposal, while other states are reviewing it.

Authored by Sydney Health Law research affiliate Neil Francey, the proposal argues the states could file proceedings in the federal court seeking up to $50bn in compensation for health costs, and to fund cancer screening programs and prevention measures.
It targets the dominant tobacco companies in Australia – British American Tobacco (BAT), Philip Morris and Imperial Brands – and their parent corporations overseas.

Francey is presenting the blueprint at the Clinical Oncology Society of Australia’s annual scientific meeting in Sydney on Thursday, arguing the companies could be held liable for decades of misleading and deceptive conduct under Australian consumer law.
He has also briefed state government MPs. Under the plan, the six state governments would pool their resources to set up a dedicated, joint legal taskforce to run the case.
“For decades, the tobacco industry has unjustly enriched itself while distracting and confusing smokers about the harms and addictiveness of their product,” the proposal says.

“The industry has not been forced to bear the full costs of the harm caused by their product. These costs have either been borne by smokers themselves, or by taxpayers when smokers get sick and receive publicly funded or subsidised health care.”
A BAT Australia spokesperson said the company does not comment on potential or pending legal claims, while Philip Morris and Imperial Brands did not respond to requests for comment.

Francey told Guardian Australia that the proposal excludes the Northern Territory and the ACT, as the territories are an arm of the commonwealth, and there are differences in healthcare funding arrangements that could complicate the case.

The proposal seeks to recover healthcare costs incurred by the states since 2000, when internal tobacco industry documents were published revealing the industry knew that smoking caused serious diseases but colluded to cover up and obfuscate the evidence.
“I think you can justify a figure in the order of fifty billion, possibly even more,” Francey said.

In 1991, Francey represented consumers in a federal court of Australia case triggered by a Tobacco Institute of Australia advertisement that claimed there was “nothing which proves scientifically that cigarette smoke causes disease in nonsmokers”.

The court found compelling scientific proof that passive smoking causes lung disease and respiratory conditions in non-smokers, making the industry’s claims unlawful. The historic ruling accelerated workplace and public indoor smoking bans.

Francey said his latest proposal has the benefit of being brought by state governments under consumer protection laws, bypassing some of the challenges faced by smokers pursuing personal injury lawsuits, where it can be hard to prove which brand caused the harm, and with tobacco companies arguing people have “freedom of choice”.
Francey said state governments could seek court orders against companies engaged in misleading and deceptive conduct which has led to loss and damage and the likelihood of suffering in future.

The South Australian health minister, Blair Boyer, said there was a “substantial” public interest in measures reducing the harms that tobacco-related diseases place on governments, health systems and communities.
“While this proposal draws on historic findings regarding misleading and deceptive conduct by the tobacco industry, it is important that the state does its own due diligence,” he said.
“I have sought advice on the proposal, the likelihood of success and the benefits to South Australians, which will allow the government to consider its options.”
A spokesperson for the NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said: “We will review his proposal carefully”.

A spokesperson for the Queensland health minister, Tim Nicholls, confirmed a meeting with Francey, but said the state was focused on laws targeting the illicit tobacco and vape trade. The Western Australian health minister, Meredith Hammat, said the state’s efforts are currently focused on strengthening tobacco legislation and enforcement activities.

The CEO of the Australian Council on Smoking & Health, Laura Hunter, said it would be “entirely reasonable for tobacco companies to bear the costs of the harm their products have caused” in Australia.

“For years, they’ve made money selling products that addict people and cause serious illness and death,” she said. “The responsibility for addressing that harm belongs with the companies that profited from it.”

The legal push follows cases overseas, including the landmark 1998 Master Settlement Agreement signed by major US tobacco companies and state attorneys general to settle dozens of lawsuits seeking to recover billions in smoking-related healthcare costs.

In 2025, three of the biggest tobacco companies were ordered to pay billions in compensation for smoking-related harms in Canada, though health groups expressed disappointment that the decision did not address harms from future use.

A professor of tobacco control with the University of Sydney, Becky Freeman, said the Canadian case was protracted over many years, and that any country taking on tobacco companies needed to ensure they were on “solid ground” to avoid spiralling costs and lacklustre outcomes.
“I am absolutely supportive of the tobacco industry being held accountable,” she said.
“I would want to ensure any action was comprehensive.”

Associate Prof Jonathan Liberman, an expert in law and global health at the University of Melbourne who has spent more than two decades working on legal aspects of tobacco control, said what has made tobacco litigation challenging is the scale and duration of the tobacco industry’s wrongdoing, and how vigorously the industry has defended it.

A range of features of the US legal system make large-scale litigation easier there, he said. To be successful in Australia, litigation against the tobacco industry over the health costs of smoking would need specific enabling legislation, and well resourced law firms working outside government doing the bulk of the necessary legal work, he said.

“Without these, lawsuits risk consuming significant time and public resources that may be better directed toward direct policy reform, and ultimately falling over on a combination of procedural grounds and resources running out.”

articles.title: [OPINION] Why ‘Trump Out’?
articles.summary: It's not because we hate America. It's because we don’t want to be its military outpost anymore, its source of cheap labor and resources, or its faraway battlefield.

blocks.text: When US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila next week for the 49th ASEAN Summit, he will be greeted not only by the red carpet rolled but by the Philippine government but by the red flags and banners of thousands of Filipinos protesting his visit.
Under the slogan “Trump Out,” various activist groups, people’s organizations and social movements have declared 12 days of protest from November 4 until Trump’s arrival on Monday, November 16.
Why protest the visit of the leader of a country that our government considers its closest and most important ally?

Trump is arguably the most racist, misogynistic, arrogant, and self-serving president in modern US history. And that’s from the point of view of many Americans themselves as shown by the result of the recent US midterm elections.
His political career has been built on demonizing immigrants, vilifying Muslims, degrading women, attacking minorities, and cultivating fear and hatred on those he considers enemies.

His administration’s brutal crackdown on undocumented immigrants has torn families apart, militarized communities, and subjected suspected people of color to arbitrary detention and deportation. His attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion, particularly surrounding gender, race, religion, and reproductive rights have emboldened right wing forces who want to reverse decades of social progress.

Trump’s misogyny is not merely a matter of offensive language. His repeated degradation of women and attacks on their rights, plus membership in the so-called Epstein class, reveal a worldview that upholds male domination and privilege.

Nor is his corruption simply a matter of rhetoric. He was convicted of 34 counts of falsifying business records. He makes no qualms about mixing public office, private business interests, and personal political loyalty, raising serious conflict of interest issues and questions about his abuse of power.
Most alarming is Trump’s authoritarianism.

He has repeatedly attacked the press, demonized political opponents, undermined democratic institutions, and encouraged the politics of intimidation. His refusal to accept defeat in the 2020 elections caused the January 6, 2021 assault on the US Capitol.

Trump’s rule bear the hallmarks of a fascistic political project: extreme nationalism, racism, a strongman cult, contempt for democratic accountability, and the use of state power to silence dissent. Surely, Filipinos who endured the Marcos dictatorship recognize the danger and reject such kind of politics.
Trump claims to be a peacemaker. But his actions show the opposite.

In total disregard of his promise to end America’s forever wars and in flagrant violation of international law, he has pursued a policy of military aggression, coercive sanctions, and intervention against countries that refuse to submit to Washington’s dictates.

From the genocide in Gaza to the senseless war on Iran, from the economic strangulation of Cuba to the hostage of Venezuela and other Caribbean countries, from his “Donroe Doctrine” to his cold war with China, Trump’s foreign policy shows the willingness of the world’s most advanced and powerful military to impose US interests through force.

His support for Israel exposes the US’s hypocrisy as a champion of human rights and international law. Same for the continued use of economic sanctions against Iran, Cuba and Venezuela that punish entire populations while claiming to promote freedom and democracy.

Far from promoting peace, Trump is accelerating a global arms race, demanding increased military spending from allies, and treating international relations as a contest of military and economic domination.

As usual, the US military-industrial complex, giant energy corporations, big tech, financial institutions, and other powerful interests stand to profit from it all while ordinary people — workers, farmers, women, children, and entire communities whose lives and livelihoods are destroyed by bombs, blockades, sanctions, and forced displacement — suffer.

As Filipinos, we have every reason to oppose Trump’s wars. We have a painful history of American colonial conquest, military intervention, and support for dictatorships. How can we possibly welcome an American president whose foreign policies are a throwback to the colonial era?

The most compelling reason for us to protest Trump’s visit is what he intends to do to our country vis a vis China. Under the Marcos regime, the Philippines has become a crucial platform for America’s strategic competition with our most powerful neighbor.

The expansion of US access to nine of our military bases under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), expanded and neverending joint military exercises, deployment of advanced missile systems and drone facilities, establishment of military warehouse and logistics hubs, and growing integration of our armed forces into the US Pacific Command have pushed our country to the frontlines of the escalating US-China rivalry.

This is especially dangerous given the unresolved territorial and maritime disputes in the West Philippine Sea. Our legitimate maritime concerns are being used to justify an increasingly militarized confrontation with China, with our fisherfolk, coast guard and navy bearing the consequences of a conflict between the two major powers.

The US is not strengthening and expanding its military presence in our islands out of an altruistic concern for our fisherfolk or our sovereignty. It’s strategic objective is to contain China’s rise as a superpower, preserve US military dominance in Asia, and secure access to the region’s vital sea lanes, markets, resources, and infrastructure.
Then there’s Trump’s weaponization of our industrial development.

The proposed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone in Tarlac aims to integrate the Philippines into US-controlled supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other ingredients for the new arms race involving artificial intelligence.

blocks.caption: No Pax Silica deal at ASEAN Summit, says US envoy

blocks.text: It remains to be seen whether Pax Silica will lead to the development of genuine Filipino industries or create decent and sustainable jobs. What is more likely is that our land, labor, energy, water, and natural resources will be used as cheap inputs for US big tech and military-industrial partners.

What will happen to the indigenous peoples, farming communities and the environment affected by Pax Silica? Who will control these AI hubs, their resources and technologies? Will these dual-use facilities serve as military targets in a future US-China war?

The “Trump Out” protests target Trump and his unhinged regime. Rather than an expression of hostility, it is an act of solidarity with the American people who just last week voted overwhelmingly to reject Trump’s authoritarianism, racism, and wars.
Real friendship with the US requires resisting its imperialist agenda, which hurt both Americans and Filipinos and other peoples of the world.

Trump, of course, is only the tip of the iceberg. US foreign policy transcends administrations and political parties. But we have to start somewhere and fight the battles that come our way any which way we can.

Trump’s visit is a chance to assert our dignity as a sovereign nation. We say “Trump Out” not because we hate America, but because we don’t want to be its military outpost anymore, its source of cheap labor and resources, or its faraway battlefield. – Rappler.com

Teddy Casiño served as Bayan Muna’s partylist representative from 2004-2013 and was a former commissioner of the EDSA People Power Commission. He is the current chairperson of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan, a alliance of nationalist and democratic peoples’ organizations and movements in the Philippines.
