articles.title: Jays' Anthony Santander stays quiet after team asks him to publicly address anti-Muslim social media posts
articles.summary: The Toronto Blue Jays have asked Anthony Santander to publicly address the controversy sparked by his decision to share anti-Muslim posts on social media. So far, the veteran outfielder has remained…

image.caption: Jays' slugger Anthony Santander shared a series of anti-Muslim posts in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections last week before deleting them two days later. (Phelan M. Ebenhack/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

The Toronto Blue Jays have asked Anthony Santander to publicly address the controversy sparked by his decision to share anti-Muslim posts on social media. So far, the veteran outfielder has remained quiet and hasn't issued an apology.
Santander shared a series of anti-Muslim videos in the aftermath of U.S. midterm election results
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 11, 2026 5:38 PM EST | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago
Barring a statement or player availability, the storyline — now in its second week — could very well extend into spring training next year.

In the meantime, a franchise that prides itself on inclusiveness has been criticized for not taking firm action, while the player appears disengaged after upsetting many team supporters and the Muslim community.
"In situations like these, the apology for some stakeholders wouldn't be good enough, but at least it's something," said Mike Naraine, a sport management associate professor at Brock University.
"To not say anything is to remain complicit in the behaviour."

items: Blue Jays player faces backlash after reposting Islamophobic content on social media following U.S. midterms

blocks.text: Santander shared posts in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections last week before deleting them two days later.

The videos included a Christian preacher saying, “There is no such thing as kind Muslims,” with another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the U.S. after Abdul El-Sayed was elected to the Senate in Michigan.
No words to express disappointment, Jays GM says
The Blue Jays provided a general statement last week and general manager Ross Atkins was asked about the controversy by reporters on Tuesday at Major League Baseball's GM meetings in Las Vegas.
"There really aren't words to express my level of disappointment," said Atkins, who added he talked to Santander and told him he should address things publicly.

items: Blue Jays response to Santander’s Islamophobic reposts ‘not enough’ for some fans
'Deeply disappointing': Jays GM Atkins weighs in on Santander's anti-Muslim posts

blocks.text: Messages left with Santander and his sports management agency on Wednesday weren't immediately returned.

"Athletes have a voice," Naraine said. "Athletes are humans as we know, and they're allowed to express their views and we love athletes for that. But when their views are rooted in bigotry or racism or transphobia or Islamophobia — as they were in this case — then it doesn't make it OK.
"It makes it incorrect, it makes it wrong and it demonstrates the exclusionary view that the athlete has."
Social media posts can bring consequences: agent
Santander, a 32-year-old from Venezuela, didn't play at the big-league level last season due to injuries. He signed a five-year, US$92.5-million deal with Toronto in January 2025.

The Blue Jays are the only MLB team in Canada, which has a population of over 1.78 million Muslims, per 2021 census data from Statistics Canada. About 10 per cent of Toronto's 2.8 million residents identify as Muslim, the agency said.

"I think some people might be surprised at just how many Muslims are fans of baseball and the Blue Jays, and Toronto is a massive sports city," said Steven Zhou, media and communications lead for the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM).
"The kind of response I've gotten from our community members from different circles, from various people, has been unbelievable. People are very, very upset."

Unanswered questions remained about how potential social media policy and morality clause contract violations might be handled. Messages left with the Blue Jays and team owner Rogers Communications Inc., weren't immediately returned. (The Canadian Press/Chris Young)
Zhou said the NCCM is open to meeting with Santander and team officials, adding he felt the situation could be an opportunity to develop and strengthen relationships with the community.

Unanswered questions remained about how potential social media policy and morality clause contract violations might be handled. Messages left with the Blue Jays and team owner Rogers Communications Inc., weren't immediately returned.
Longtime agent Brian Levine, who primarily works with Olympians, said an athlete's social media posts can have real contractual and financial consequences.

"I don't know if these traditional professional team sport athletes get a little too comfortable with the compensation they get, if they feel untouchable, if they're just not thinking, if there's poor media training," said Levine, who founded Toronto-based Envision Sports & Entertainment.

"Like let's be honest, did the Blue Jays not sit down these players and give them a rulebook of do's and don'ts at the beginning of the season? That's what really baffles me, is this is pretty basic stuff."
Parting of ways unlikely: lawyer
Santander hit 44 homers for the Baltimore Orioles in 2024 but hit just .175 with six homers over 54 games in an injury-plagued 2025 season with Toronto.
He's expected to be healthy for the 2027 season and become an everyday player again.

items: Muslim group calls Santander posts disconcerting, says there's an opportunity at hand
Blue Jays front office speaks after end of disappointing season

blocks.text: "It would not surprise me to see discipline of some kind," said lawyer Elliot Saccucci of Toronto-based Loopstra Nixon LLP, who added a parting of ways could be possible although unlikely.

"I don't know if Rogers has the appetite to spend [about 63] million dollars to release this player," said Saccucci, who's head of the firm's sports law group. "They might and they're not losing much [productivity] on the field.
"But that's a significant financial commitment for somebody that's not going to be with your team."
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the joint intelligence committee, will take on the role of advising No 10 on climate-related national security risks

The UK government has appointed…
articles.byline: Fiona Harvey in Antalya and Damien Gayle in London

blocks.text: The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

Prime minister Andy Burnham will announce the move on Thursday at Cop31, the UN climate summit, with the new role designed to advise the government on national security risks from the climate crisis before they spell catastrophe.

Burnham will tell the key climate talks on Thursday morning: “We should all recognise the summer was not normal. The climate crisis is upon all of us now. We saw that with the wildfires that devastated lives and livelihoods everywhere.”

This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, with back-to-back heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis causing health services and transport to suffer, schools to close and thousands of people to lose their lives prematurely.

Burnham will add: “The message I carry here, in my first Cop as prime minister, is that the UK remains determined to reach net zero by 2050 and to work with our partners to build a clean energy future. The world has changed. The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate action has broken down.
“We will not stand by, and that’s why I’ve pledged a new era of British leadership over the next decade.”

blocks.caption: UK climate group Mothers Rise Up protest near Downing Street in September to highlight the impact of record-breaking heat on children. Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Burnham arrived in Antalya, Turkey late on Wednesday night, before joining scores of heads of state and government for a series of high-level meetings at the talks, which are presided over jointly by Turkey and Australia. He will also confirm UK support for a proposed target of 35% electrification by 2035 and help towards plans to raise £5bn in private finance for clean energy projects across the world.
Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the UK’s joint intelligence committee (JIC), which oversees MI5 and MI6, will take on the special representative job.

But campaigners pointed to what they said were Burnham’s failures to take the measures needed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions at home, and to provide the funding needed to protect vulnerable countries overseas from the kind of risks the JIC has warned about. The government is mulling a major weakening of targets for electric vehicles and has given the green light to a gasfield, Jackdaw, in the North Sea while considering a new oilfield, Rosebank, west of Shetland.

blocks.caption: Climate campaigners protest outside the Department of Energy and Net Zero against the decision drilling at Jackdaw and Rosebank. Photograph: Denise Baker/Getty Images

blocks.text: “What we’re seeing in part is double standards,” Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, told the Guardian. “We can’t have Britain preaching a clean development gospel but expanding fossil fuels back at home. You cannot expect one set of rules for Africa and another for Britain.”

The UK’s credibility was “crumbling”, said Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth England, Wales and Northern Ireland. “The prime minister’s first climate talks should be an opportunity to demonstrate he means business. But if this is all the UK has to offer, then the questions piling in about his climate credibility are more than justified.”

Under Alessandri, the JIC collaborated on a secret report warning that within five years the UK could begin experiencing national security impacts from the collapse of ecosystems overseas, driven by the climate crisis and overexploitation of the living world. These impacts included food shortages, rising food prices, mass migration and conflict among nuclear-armed countries.
The report was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer, but its contents were revealed by the Guardian last year, ahead of a redacted publication earlier this year.

Dame Madeleine Alessandri said: “Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates, placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world.

“The best time to address these risks is before they develop into crises. In this role, I will work with partners across government and internationally to strengthen our understanding of climate threats, build resilience and ensure we are better prepared for the challenges ahead.”

blocks.caption: Low water levels in Colliford Lake reservoir, Bodmin Moor, Cornwall. This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record.  Photograph: Amazing Aerial/Alamy

blocks.text: The risks of the climate crisis to national security were also highlighted by Ed Miliband, foreign secretary, who has been briefing foreign capitals on the findings of the JIC report. He is also at Cop31 this week, and told the Guardian: “National security is the next frontier of the fight for climate action – the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences in the daily news.”
He added: “Climate breakdown is one of the greatest national security threats we face: food security, threats to infrastructure and population movements [are resulting from the climate crisis].
“Those who seek to stick their heads in the sand on climate are putting our national security at risk.”

In common with many wealthy nations, the UK has significantly rolled back its climate finance, funnelling money instead to military spending. In July, Burnham fronted a pledge to lower the cap on UK bus fares, funded by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.

Prakash Dahal of Pro Public and Friends of the Earth Nepal said finance was vital for his country’s adaptation to climate breakdown, and recovery from disasters such as the catastrophic flash flood that struck Nepal in August. “Crucially, this essential funding must come as grants – not loans,” he said. “Nepal is not asking for charity. Nepal is demanding justice.”

articles.title: Halifax’s Brian Ahern, who produced albums by Anne Murray and Johnny Cash, dead at 81
articles.summary: A Halifax-born music producer who played a big role in helping encourage fellow Bluenoser Anne Murray to pursue a career in music and later produced albums by artists such as Johnny Cash and Emmylou…

image.caption: Emmylou Harris, Brian Ahern and Rodney Crowell accept the Album of the Year award at the Americana Music Honors And Awards on Sept. 18, 2013, in Nashville. Ahern also won a Grammy in 2014 for Best Americana Album for the same record, Old Yellow Moon. (Rick Diamond/Getty Images for Americana Music Fe

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

A Halifax-born music producer who played a big role in helping encourage fellow Bluenoser Anne Murray to pursue a career in music and later produced albums by artists such as Johnny Cash and Emmylou Harris is being remembered for the mark he left on the music industry.
'We kind of cut our teeth and grew up in the music business together,' says Anne Murray
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 11, 2026 5:13 PM EST | Last Updated: 17 minutes ago
Brian Ahern, 81, died Monday at a care home in Minnesota.

Murray said she met Ahern when she auditioned for Singalong Jubilee, a CBC television program featuring local artists in Halifax that ran in the 1960s and 1970s. Ahern was the musical producer on the show. Murray said she did not make the cut the first time she auditioned.
"He wanted me to be on that show," Murray told CBC Wednesday. "And that's where it all started with Brian."
She was invited to audition again two years later and succeeded.
Anne Murray of Springhill, N.S., is shown in a 1971 photo. (The Canadian Press)
Ahern later moved to Toronto, while Murray remained on the East Coast working as a teacher. She did not feel ready to become a full-time musician, but Ahern kept pushing her.

"He was at me, writing letters, begging me to come to Toronto to do an album. Well, I couldn't see the point in that at all," said Murray with a laugh. "Finally, I gave in and I gave up teaching and went to Toronto and we did an album together."
She said he was very quiet and called him a brilliant musician.

"And sometimes you have to read his mind ... but he taught me a lot in the studio," said Murray. "I learned a lot from him as he was learning too, but he was so smart that he got to the point pretty quickly."

They faced many challenges together. When Murray arrived in Toronto, she said Ahern had "no money" and that she had to get his guitar back using money made from teaching before they could record in a studio.
Brian Ahern accepts a lifetime achievement award for producer/engineer during The Americana Music Awards in Nashville on Sept. 9, 2010. (The Associated Press)
"We kind of cut our teeth and grew up in the music business together," said Murray.
Her breakout song, Snowbird, from 1969's This Way Is My Way, was one of 13 albums he produced by Murray, according to the Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame.
Murray said the two "went [their] separate ways, but [they] both went on to greater things."
From left: Ricky Skaggs, Emmylou Harris and Brian Ahern perform on Nov. 18, 2013, in Nashville. (Rick Diamond/Getty Images)

Ahern's work also took him to places such as Los Angeles, and Nashville. He also produced albums by George Jones, Ricky Skaggs and Rodney Crowell. He also produced 11 of Emmylou Harris's albums; the pair married in 1974.
The last time Murray saw Ahern in person was when he was inducted into the Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame in 2006.
"Brian's confidence in my ability was enough to carry me through those early years," Murray said before introducing Ahern on stage.
In 2010, he was awarded a lifetime achievement awards by the Americana Music Association and became a member of the Order of Canada in 2019.

In a statement following his death, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum said Ahern's work "helped create an essential form of American roots music" and it "provided a blueprint for Americana music in the 1990s."
Ahern was a 'steward of the artistic process'
Ahern's daughters, Shannon and Meghann Ahern, said they have fond memories of sleeping in recording studios as kids while their father worked.

"He would just take us everywhere, and he would build me like a human-sized dollhouse out of the studio baffles (soundproofing equipment), so I would have a way to play and keep myself quiet while he was working," said Shannon Ahern.
They described him as a "steward of the artistic process" who took his job seriously to ensure artists reached their full creative potential.

"They were people who I understood as being talented musicians, and that my dad was making art with them," said Meghann Ahern. "That was my context, that art was important, but it also required a work ethic and commitment and dedication."

articles.title: Deadline nears to claim piece of $11-million CIBC mutual funds settlement
articles.summary: Investors who held units of a CIBC mutual fund or a Renaissance mutual fund on or before Sept. 5, 2025 might be eligible for compensation. The deadline to apply is Nov. 18.

image.caption: The CIBC logo is displayed on a flag in front of the bank's headquarters in Toronto in 2021. The deadline is nearing to apply for a class-action settlement involving CIBC mutual funds. (Evan Buhler/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New
Investors who held units of a CIBC mutual fund or a Renaissance mutual fund on or before Sept. 5, 2025 might be eligible for compensation. The deadline to apply is Nov. 18.
Investors who held CIBC or Renaissance mutual funds on or before Sept. 5, 2025 might be eligible
If you've bought CIBC mutual funds, you might be eligible for a piece of an $11-million settlement — and the deadline to apply is fast approaching.

Anyone who held units of a CIBC mutual fund or a Renaissance mutual fund on or before Sept. 5, 2025 is eligible for compensation, except those investors who held the funds through a discount broker. (Renaissance Investments is a subsidiary of CIBC.)

The class-action lawsuit alleges that trailing commissions were incorrectly paid out to discount brokers — those like Scotia iTRADE or Wealthsimple, which let investors execute trades but don't usually provide personalized financial planning.

Trailing commissions are paid to mutual fund dealers or advisers to compensate for their advice. The class action alleged that since no advice is given by discount brokers, the fees are "excessive, inflated and/or unearned."

CIBC was also allegedly paying those trailing commissions with funds from its mutual fund assets. The settlement isn't an admission of guilt by CIBC or the CIBC Trust Corporation — the asset management wing of CIBC also named in the lawsuit.
This TD customer lost over $450K to bank fraud. Why isn't the bank held accountable? | Go Public

Anyone who is eligible for the settlement and currently holds CIBC or Renaissance mutual funds will be refunded automatically — no claim necessary — with their cut of the settlement deposited directly into their existing mutual funds.
But former CIBC mutual fund holders will have to submit a claim form by Nov. 18 to be eligible. That can be done online on the class-action site.
Those who held both CIBC mutual funds and Renaissance mutual funds might be compensated for both of those claims, the class-action site says.

It's unclear exactly how much claimants could get from the settlement, but the plan of allocation shows it could be about $32, as long as there are enough funds to pay each eligible person who made a claim.

articles.title: Quebec government to table bill restricting access to English-language colleges
articles.summary: Next year will mark half a century since the adoption of Quebec's Charter of the French Language, and the Parti Québécois government intends to mark the milestone by reforming the law, says Pascal…

image.caption: Pascal Bérubé, Quebec's minister of the French language, says the government is 'counting on everybody to make sure that the French language still has vitality and is there forever.' (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal

Next year will mark half a century since the adoption of Quebec's Charter of the French Language, and the Parti Québécois government intends to mark the milestone by reforming the law, says Pascal Bérubé, the minister of the French language.
Next year marks 50 years of Quebec's Charter of the French Language

Next year will mark half a century since the adoption of Quebec's Charter of the French Language, and the Parti Québécois (PQ) government intends to mark the milestone by reforming the law, says Pascal Bérubé, the minister of the French language.

Bérubé reminded reporters at the National Assembly on Wednesday that 2027 will see the PQ government table a bill to further protect French. The legislation would include "strong" measures, such as restricting English-language CEGEPs, or junior colleges, to students who are legally eligible to study in English.
"We are counting on everybody to make sure that the French language still has vitality and is there forever," Bérubé said.
As a minority government, the PQ would need the support of at least one opposition party to adopt legislation.

Quebec's French Language Charter mandates that children of francophones or allophones attend French-language elementary and high schools when enrolled in the public education network, with only those who qualify for a certificate of eligibility for instruction in English being exempted.

items: Montreal's LaSalle College gets more time to settle debts amid language fines dispute

blocks.text: Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has openly shared his support for extending these eligibility restrictions to Quebec's English-language CEGEP network, a plan that was also included in the PQ's electoral platform.
Bérubé repeated that the government intends to support the renewal of the notwithstanding clause on Bill 96, Quebec's language law, which is set to expire next June.

The notwithstanding clause allows provincial governments to enact legislation that limits sections of Canada's Charter of Rights and Freedoms for a maximum of five years, unless renewed by legislators.
Respecting Quebecers' freedom of choice

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said his party would not support a measure forcing adults to study in a specific language, particularly when current laws already require francophones and allophones to attend public schools in French.
"Adults should make their own decisions," Duhaime said. "We do believe that you cannot oblige adults to go to an institution in the language of the choice of the government."
Students typically begin CEGEP courses after graduating from high school at 17, with pre-university and technical programs lasting between two and three years.

items: Groups decry Quebec's proposed ban on school kids wearing religious symbols

blocks.text: For the Quebec Liberals, restricting access to English-language CEGEPs would not increase the number of French speakers or help French flourish in the province, says Madwa-Nika Cadet, the party's critic for the French language, francization and integration.

"What it does is prevent francophones and allophones from frequenting higher-learning institutions in the language of their choice at a moment when they are already French speakers," Cadet said in an interview with CBC's Quebec AM on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Québec Solidaire confirmed on Wednesday that the party is against applying the Charter at the CEGEP level, noting that it respects adults' freedom of choice.
With files from CBC's Cathy Senay

articles.title: Fears of rising antisemitism in Europe
articles.summary: Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny commemorates the victims of Auschwitz as Jewish communities across Europe face growing hostility. What does the promise of "Never Again" mean for Jewish life in…

image.caption: The infamous line 'Work sets you free' (Arbeit macht frei) is written on the iron gateway to AuschwitzImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Regina Sluszny makes her way in her wheelchair through the iron gate marking the entrance to the former Auschwitz concentration camp. "I feel the cold, both physically and emotionally," says the 87-year-old Jewish woman, her gaze fixed on the grey horizon.

How many times has she been here? Six, seven, perhaps eight, she estimates. And each time, the same thoughts run through her mind: "I think about my husband's family. He lost seven loved ones here. They were sent straight to the gas chambers and murdered."

blocks.caption: Regina Sluszny has spent four decades sharing her story with school childrenImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Regina Sluszny traveled to Poland with a delegation from the European Jewish Association (EJA), a European advocacy group representing Jewish interests that regularly organizes conferences on Jewish life as well as visits to former concentration camps.

This year, the organization invited political representatives and members of Jewish communities to Krakow and Auschwitz on November 9 and 10. The trip was deliberately scheduled to coincide with the anniversary of the November Pogroms of 1938, widely regarded as a watershed moment on the path to the Holocaust.

"Honoring the past, securing the future" is the event's motto. Like many others in attendance, Holocaust survivor Regina Sluszny fears that the horrors of the Shoah are slowly fading from Europe's collective memory.

blocks.caption: A delegation of the European Jewish Association visits the former Auschwitz concentration camp Image: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Persian-Jewish ties

Among this year's international religious and political representatives, the guest of honor was Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah and a prominent opponent of the Islamic Republic. The European Jewish Association (EJA) honored him for his efforts to combat antisemitism.
Accepting the award, Pahlavi recalled the historic ties between the Persian and Jewish peoples and called on democratic nations around the world to unite against oppression and ideological extremism.

But talking to attendees at the symposium in Krakow, it quickly becomes clear that fear of rising antisemitism is much closer to home. Many describe growing hostility towards Jews and rising fear in Jewish communities across Europe.
In France, authorities recorded a total of 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025. That was fewer than in 2024, but around three times as many as in 2022.

In Germany, the number of antisemitic crimes recorded by police rose from 2,641 in 2022 to 6,236 in 2024 and 6,548 in 2025. Authorities and monitoring organizations across Europe have reported a significant increase in antisemitic incidents since October 7, 2023.

For Ellen van Praagh, chair of the Interprovincial Rabbinate in the Netherlands, October 7, 2023, marked a turning point. She also lost a family member during the Hamas-led attack which saw around 1,200 people in Israel killed and over 250 taken hostage and abducted to the Gaza Strip.

blocks.caption: Around six million Jews were murdered during the HolocaustImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: 'We want to live in freedom'

"My family has lived in the Netherlands since the 16th century. And now I'm being told to leave," says van Praagh. She says the atmosphere in the Netherlands has changed dramatically since the attack. She no longer feels safe there as a Jew. "We Jews are being held responsible for Israel's actions."

Israel launched a major military offensive in the Gaza Strip after the October-7 attack. More than 75,000 Palestinians have been killed there since the start of the war, according to conservative estimates.

Like many others at the symposium, van Praagh says she is increasingly losing faith in politicians. "Never Again" has become an empty phrase, she argues, with little relevance to the everyday lives of Jews in Europe.
Jewish communities now have to protect themselves behind high walls. Constant security measures restrict their daily lives, she explains. "That is not what we want. We want to live in freedom."

Rabbi Menachem Margolin, chairman of the European Jewish Association, is also calling on European political leaders to take greater responsibility. He says he is grateful for their support, without which Jewish life in Europe would hardly be possible.

However, laws designed to protect Jewish life are often not enforced in practice. Many officials hesitate to call antisemitism by its name as soon as doing so becomes politically inconvenient. "But Auschwitz did not begin with gas chambers. It began with words," he cautioned.
A visit to Auschwitz-Birkenau — the Holocaust death factory
At the Birkenau memorial

Regina Sluszny joined the delegation visiting the Birkenau memorial. The Auschwitz concentration and extermination camp, built by Nazi Germany, became a symbol of the Holocaust. The Nazis murdered around 1.1 million people there, including approximately one million Jews. Most were killed here at Birkenau.

The delegation is gathered to commemorate the November Pogroms of November 9 and 10, 1938, when Nazis set synagogues on fire, ransacked Jewish businesses and homes and murdered Jews. Around 30,000 Jewish men were deported to concentration camps.

Survivors like Regina are increasingly rare. Most Holocaust survivors have passed away. Regina survived because, in 1942, a family friend and his wife took her in when she was just two years old while her parents fled the Nazis with her two brothers and went into hiding.

For more than 40 years, she has been sharing her story with schoolchildren, doing her part to ensure that the Holocaust is never forgotten. For her, "Never Again" is a promise that must be kept. Otherwise, it becomes a lie.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: B.C. search-and-rescue mule using his nose to help solve Arizona cold case
articles.summary: A British Columbia mule with a nose that knows is helping investigators trying to crack a missing persons cold case in Arizona.

image.caption: Marion Weisskopff and Sonny search the Arizona backcountry. (Marion Weisskopff)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
A British Columbia mule with a nose that knows is helping investigators trying to crack a missing persons cold case in Arizona.
Sonny, who is part of Princeton search-and-rescue team, is using his scent detection training for 1st time
A British Columbia mule with a nose that knows is helping investigators trying to crack a cold case in Arizona.
Chelsea Grimm vanished while on a cross-country road trip in 2023. Her vehicle was found abandoned on a forest service road in the Kaibab National Forest, just south of the Grand Canyon.

Now, Sonny, a scent-detecting mule, and his human, Princeton Ground Search and Rescue (PGSAR) volunteer Marion Weiskopff, have joined in a private search to try and find any trace of the missing woman.
LISTEN | This search-and-rescue mule from Princeton is using his nose to help solve a cold case:
Daybreak South7:33Princeton SAR volunteer and her scent detecting mule search for a missing woman in Arizona
Weiskopff and Sonny are a part of B.C.'s only dedicated mounted search-and-rescue team, but this is the first time they've been called on for his scent detection skills.

"When he picks up a smell, he stops dead in his tracks and he takes the air in, like you can hear him sniffing the air, and then he just turns [to] where the scent is coming from," Weiskopff explained.
Sonny the mule and Marion Weisskopff are handed an award for winning a scenting field trial in Oregon in 2024. (Marion Weisskopff)
Sonny honed those abilities at training clinics in Oregon and Arizona several years ago, and went on to win equine scenting competitions in each state, Weiskopff told CBC's Daybreak South.
"Sonny found the scent in about a 10-acre plot in under a minute and a half," she explained. "Other horses often take 10 minutes and longer."
A missing person poster for Chelsea Grimm seen in Arizona. (Marion Weisskopff)
Arizona search
Private investigator Steve Fishcher, who is working the search for Grimm, learned about Sonny through contacts in the search-and-rescue community.

When he learned that Weiskopff and her husband spend several months a year in Arizona with Sonny and their horses, he invited them to help scour a 400-square kilometre slice of the Arizona backcountry.
Marion Weiskopff and Sonny (right) and her husband Don and his SAR-certified horse Mariah (left) search the Arizona backcountry. (Marion Weiskopff)
It's also a first for Fischer, who said while he's familiar with scent-detecting equines, he hasn't employed them before.

"Another team out of Florida called Peace River Search and Rescue, who I've been involved in searches with and who I really respect, they have an equine division ... they even have a scent otter for underwater searches," he said.
"So when the opportunity came up, I was very interested in it."
Private investigator Steve Fischer on the site of the search for Chelsea Grimm as mounted teams assemble. (@SF_investigates / X)
Fischer said horses and mules add "great value" to search efforts because of the terrain they can cover.
Previous searches of the area using ATVs, drones and even cadaver dogs have come up empty handed.

"Being able to have those equines get into some of those areas that have been really difficult for us on foot is gonna give us the best chance and hopefully finding Chelsea if she's out there," he said.
Weiskopff said the goal of the current search is to find any possessions or remains that could help bring closure to Grimm's family.
A piece of shoe that Sonny helped locate in the Arizona backcountry. (Marion Weisskopff)
"The mule actually found a torn off shoe, the bottom of a shoe, and it was a lady size shoe in the middle of nowhere, it wasn't near a trail or anything, and he took me right too that," she said.
"But because it's just a sole they can't really identify if it was Chelsea's or not."
Heavy rain and mud forced them to suspend the mounted search for safety reasons, Fischer said he hopes to do another large-scale search in drier weather.
Mounted SAR team
While this is the first time Sonny has specifically put his nose to work, he and Weiskopff are no strangers to search-and-rescue work.
They're part of PGSAR's mounted search-and-rescue unit, composed of five trained volunteers with their own mounts, who master an additional list of 60 tasks for certification.
The Princeton Ground Search and Rescue mounted team. (Princeton Ground Search and Rescue)
PGSAR president Paul Fyfe said the unit is ideal for the region's steep mountains and ranch-like grasslands.
"The horses do give a better advantage for access, but also for for view," he said.
And while scent detection isn't one of their official skills, Fyfe said it can play an informal role in search work.
"The equines give signals to anything interesting in the area through their sense of smell or through their ears," he said.
"Being prey animals [they] are much more sort of aware of their surroundings."
Fyfe said the team hasn't ruled out getting more formal scent training for the unit like Weiskopff and Sonny.
With files from Daybreak South

articles.title: African writing award probe finds 'no evidence' winning story was AI generated
articles.summary: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has also vehemently denied the allegation made in a US magazine.

blocks.text: The Caine Prize for African Writing has said that after an internal review it has found no evidence that Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza had used generative AI to write his winning short story and confirmed him as the winner of this year's £10,000 ($13,000) award.

Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees, said the matter had been investigated following an article in US magazine The Atlantic with the headline, Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI.
"From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human written," she said in a video posted on X.
The accusation had caused a social media uproar and Kundizeza had denied the allegation.
The Atlantic article by journalist Vauhini Vara alleged that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

Her allegations followed rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Following the publication of her article last month, Vara had told BBC's Front Row programme that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".
The backlash on social media included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

articles.title: Missing baby rescued after being buried alive in a dog crate in South Carolina
articles.summary: A missing 11-month-old infant was rescued Tuesday after being buried alive in a dog crate in South Carolina.

image.caption: In a photo supplied by his great aunt, 11-month-old Koah Sharp is seen sleeping Nov. 7, days before being buried alive. (Amber Hammond/Handout/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
A missing 11-month-old infant was rescued Tuesday after being buried alive in a dog crate in South Carolina.
Searchers found the infant wrapped in a towel about 24 hours after he was reported missing

A county sheriff says little Koah Sharp had been underground for about 24 hours but survived, likely due to an air pocket created by a towel wrapped around the crate. Cool temperatures may also have helped.
Dozens of first responders combed the countryside for the "bright boy with reddish blond hair" that the sheriff's office said had disappeared while his grandmother ran errands.

After a full day of searching, authorities found freshly disturbed soil in the woods not far from the home of the boy's grandfather. They began digging and soon unearthed the baby, who was "clinging to life," the sheriff said.

"Certainly, God is good," Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference, not long after Koah was found. "He was screaming at the top of his lungs, which is a good thing in the baby world, I would guess."

A photo provided by the Lexington County Sheriff's office in Lexington, S.C., shows Michael Comer in custody after his son was found buried alive. (Lexington County Sheriff's Office/The Associated Press)
The child's father, Michael Comer, 25, was arrested and was being held without bond on a burglary charge, Koon said. Investigators were working with prosecutors to confirm further charges, he said.
Koah, who disappeared Monday in the county just west of Columbia, was taken to a hospital. His condition was not immediately known Wednesday.
"We're better now that we know that Koah is safe," his great aunt, Amber Hammond, told The Associated Press in an interview. She was watching as he was freed from the crate.
100 people helped in search
Deputies who searched the grandfather's home found the doors open and baby belongings inside, but they did not see Comer or the child, the sheriff said. Then the digging started.
"It was shallow," Koon said. "It was probably about at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground."
It was not immediately known if Comer had a lawyer. A phone number could not be found for him. The Associated Press sent emails seeking information to the public defender and prosecutors.
Nearly 100 first responders participated in the search.
Authorities said Koah had been in the care of Comer's mother. She had to run an errand and left the boy in Comer's care. Another caregiver was on the way, Koon said.
"By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone, and Koah was gone with him," Koon said.

items: Quebec toddler found alive and well after intensive 4-day search, police say
B.C. man who went missing in mountains for several days found alive

blocks.text: Surveillance video from several businesses in the area showed Comer without the infant on Monday afternoon, Koon said. The father was found Monday night and was arrested.
Koah's parents "have had some situations" regarding domestic violence charges, the sheriff said.
"Children," he said, "sometimes get caught in the middle."
Montreal toddler found alive after 4-day search a rare ending, police say

Comer was sentenced to probation in October after pleading guilty to domestic violence and aggravated breach-of-peace charges related to an arrest in July, Lexington County online court records show. Prosecutors dropped a gun charge as part of the plea deal.

articles.title: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say
articles.summary:
Retailer’s management to seek two-week extension of legal protection from creditors in high court

MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the retailer…

blocks.text: MPs have accused the owner of Poundland of extracting millions of pounds from the budget retailer when it was on a “knife-edge” as it seeks extra time to secure a rescue deal.

The management of Poundland, which employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, will seek a two-week extension of legal protection from creditors from the high court on Thursday morning.

The budget chain’s owner, Gordon Brothers, is under pressure to accept a bid for the company that would save retail jobs and protect thousands of suppliers. Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators two weeks ago.
The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until Thursday morning while a solution to its problems is sought.

Directors of Poundland are now seeking a further 10 working days’ grace, which must be approved by the high court. That comes after Gordon Brothers, which is understood to be supportive of the extension, released £10m more in funds to help Poundland secure new stock and keep trading.
Without the legal protection in place, Poundland is likely to have to call in administrators; the advisory firm Alix Partners is already lined up.

The European head of Gordon Brothers, Mark Newton-Jones, gave evidence in private for almost two hours to the Commons business select committee on Wednesday afternoon after MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Liam Byrne, the chair of the committee, said that after questioning Newton-Jones he was “deeply concerned that Gordon Brothers’ behaviour may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain’s high streets”.
He said: “Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a ‘knife-edge’.
“Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there’s concerning signs it’s been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run-up to Christmas.
“Worse, Gordon Brothers refused to say it will prioritise saving jobs over and above its own financial returns.”
The committee separately heard from Poundland’s management team, led by Barry Williams, who had been fighting to save the business.

Sources said Poundland continued to trade well, with sales up year on year, despite its problems, but it only has enough cash to support the business for a short period. Gordon Brothers has said Poundland remains “challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading”.

Gordon Brothers is understood to remain in talks with three potential bidders for the entire chain but has indicated it can raise more from a break-up of Poundland, selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers.

The bids are understood to be worth less than the £30m in debts taken on by shareholders when Gordon Brothers bought the chain. It bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025.
after newsletter promotion
Pepco still holds £7.5m of the £30m shareholder debt. It is prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.

Gordon Brothers is still in talks with Martin Property Group, the Northern Irish family-owned firm supporting a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which includes the Dealz chain in Ireland.
Martin Property Group’s first bid had been rejected by Gordon Brothers as it amounted to no more than half the £30m it wants for Poundland with less than £7m up front.
A little-known finance company, Xyra Group, is thought to have offered about £12m up front and close to £30m in total. However, Xyra has not been involved with retail businesses previously.
Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Double amputee marathon runner criticises Badenoch for ‘weaponising his success’
articles.summary:
Paralympian Richard Whitehead ‘gobsmacked’ at Tory leader’s speech over proposed £36bn welfare cuts

The double amputee marathon runner

blocks.text: The double amputee marathon runner Richard Whitehead has criticised Kemi Badenoch for “weaponising his sporting success” to justify her proposed £36bn welfare cuts.

The Conservative leader used the example of “double amputees running marathons” in a speech this week to explain the reasoning behind her proposed cuts to disability benefits, which she said were enabling people to “live a life of dependency”.
Whitehead said he had been surprised at her comments and angry that his achievements were being used as part of a campaign to take money “from the most vulnerable that actually need it”.

“I was gobsmacked that somebody’s sporting success would be weaponised in this way,” he said. “To say everybody should work because double-leg amputees run marathons, I was like, wow. It’s very divisive language.

“I understand the welfare system needs a shake-up, but you shouldn’t be blanket taking money away from individuals who need it, it’s their lifeline. There are families out there relying on the support.”

blocks.caption: Kemi Badenoch claimed in her speech that disability benefits enabled people to ‘live a life of dependency’. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA

blocks.text: Whitehead has run more than 100 marathons, set world records and won four Paralympic medals over the course of his career, while also completing endurance feats to raise money for charity.
He said several people had sent him clips of Badenoch’s speech on Tuesday and “his mouth was open” as he watched it.

After saying there were “people who genuinely cannot work”, Badenoch went on to say: “The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities, even when they face serious challenges.
“Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.”

Whitehead immediately expressed his concerns about the comments on social media. “Disability should never be judged through isolated examples of individual achievement, but through an understanding of the barriers people and families face every day,” he wrote.

blocks.caption: Richard Whitehead’s medals include gold in the men’s 200m T42 final at the Rio 2016 Paralympic Games. Photograph: Matthew Stockman/Getty Images

blocks.text: “One person’s ability to overcome significant challenges should never be used to justify withdrawing support from others.”
after newsletter promotion
He invited Badenoch to have a conversation with him to learn more about disability and how it had affected his life and how he used his platform to inspire and mentor others.

“She’s utilising somebody’s success and 50 years of hard work for her own means without actually having any knowledge of who I am and the work that I do,” he said. “When I stand on a podium, I use that moment to hopefully inspire and liberate people of all minorities. She’s just looked for a headline.
“I think she needs to really reflect and think about how she communicates with the disabled community, and maybe have a conversation with myself around the work that I’m doing.”

The Conservatives said welfare savings would be made by ending disability living allowance payments to families of children with “milder cases” of behavioural disorders, learning disabilities or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Badenoch said in her speech: “If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself.”

Whitehead said: “I would like a response from her on the terminology she used and I could educate her about the real scenario for people with neurodiversity, with ADHD, who are really struggling. And maybe with that experience she will understand that maybe she’s got it wrong.”

articles.title: VW scraps production modernization plan citing tough financial straits
articles.summary: VW has announced that it will scrap large-scale modernization in light of its current economic situation. Employee representatives accuse leadership of putting short-term profits before long-term…

image.caption: VW's works council slammed the modernization U-turn as a 'flagrant breach' of the collective bargaining agreement reached in 2024Image: Hauke-Christian Dittrich/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Volkswagen, Europe's largest automaker, cited financial constraints on Wednesday when announcing that it will not carry out modernization plans as previously outlined in its project "Gamechanger" scheme.

A VW spokesman said all investments at the company are currently under review and that a planned large-scale casting facility at its main Wolfsburg site would not be moving forward despite years of preparation, investment and the stated goal of future-proofing the company for a rapidly evolving production landscape.

In his statement, the spokesman said the scrapping of Gamechanger did not mean the company would forego development of its Scalable Systems Platform (SSP) program, which aims to create a shared electric platform for future VW models like the ID. Roc, T-Roc and electric Golf.
VW, he said, will also continue to streamline production by simplifying its next generation of vehicles at all of its production facilities.
Volkswagen turns to new models, cost-cutting
What did VW employee representatives say about Gamechanger's cancellation?

Daniela Cavallo, chair of the VW works council, slammed the decision, saying it was an admission of leadership's failure and accusing CEO Oliver Blume of forfeiting all claims of technical leadership in vehicle production.
Cavallo blasted the decision as a "flagrant breach" of agreements reached during difficult collective bargain negotiations in late 2024.

The 2024 agreement between VW and its employees outlined massive investments for facilities in order to create a foundation for the production of new models at VW's German factories and the relocation of internal combustion vehicle manufacturing to VW sites in Mexico.

blocks.caption: Wolfsburg was to be the site of modern production technology including new large-scale casting facilitiesImage: Julian Stratenschulte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: VW's Wolfsburg facilities, for instance, were to be overhauled in order to initiate SSP production there by the end of the decade. The overhaul centered on state-of-the-art manufacturing technologies such as the large-scale casting of body parts on site as envisioned in the Gamechanger project.

Works Council boss Cavallo has demanded the company's board of directors give a clear statement on what the abrupt scrapping of Gamechanger will mean for workers and production volume, adding, "production of the internal combustion Golf is not leaving Wolfsburg until we get transparency on the details of the decision."

Cavallo also accused VW leadership of putting short-term financial gain for investors ahead of the wellbeing of the company and its workers, saying, "Short-term return-driven thinking now stands in the foreground, and no longer the future viability of the VW Group, as was the case for decades."
Can Volkswagen stage an automotive comeback?

articles.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
articles.summary:
74-year-old Leonardo Bertulazzi, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody

A 74-year-old former member of

blocks.text: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday.
Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence.
He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.
The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks between 1969 and 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”.
The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Local press went wild describing details of Bertulazzi’s escape from his residence in the capital, but authorities have not confirmed the veracity of any of the reports.
He reportedly used a harness to lower himself from a fifth-floor balcony.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

articles.title: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, Marshall Islands president tells Cop31
articles.summary: Hilda Heine warns of effects of catastrophic global heating as world leaders meet in Turkey amid calls for urgent action on fossil fuels
articles.byline: Oliver Milman, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn in Antalya, and Ajit Niranjan

blocks.text: Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.

Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.
She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.
“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.
“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.
“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

blocks.caption: Hilda Heine giving her speech at the Cop31 leaders’ summit, in which she told delegates: ‘It’s time to wake up.’ Photograph: Mehmet Emin Menguarslan/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.

António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.
“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”

Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.

blocks.caption: Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, addressed Cop31 days after celebrating the discovery of two new oilfields. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.

In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”

Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.

The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.
Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.

Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history, there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.

“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”

Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.

Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”
Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

articles.title: Trump planning new military assault or tighter sanctions, say Iranian officials
articles.summary:
Regime adviser says Tehran could be forced into pre-emptive strikes if stalemate continues

Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an…

blocks.text: Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic stranglehold that will push Tehran into retaliatory action.
The assessment comes from Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table. He claimed Washington was preparing for a limited strike and Iran was already preparing a response.
If the US sanctions continued, he said, a comprehensive pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”.

Mohammadi described the US response to Iran’s latest proposals on reopening the strait of Hormuz as “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive”. “They do not want to release the frozen funds,” he said. “They do not want to lift the sanctions and they do not want to stop the war in Lebanon.”

He also disclosed that Iran had rejected a request from the US vice-president, JD Vance, for a direct meeting with its negotiators before giving a response to Tehran’s conditions for lifting the siege on the strait.
For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz.

blocks.caption: A tanker burns off Oman in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, apparently after an attack by Iranian forces trying to stop oil shipments. Photograph: Social media/Reuters

blocks.text: Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year.
On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required.

Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago.

In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines.

A third senior official, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, warned Europe that any complicity in the US blockade would be “an act of war that will be etched in the nation’s historical memory”.

Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.”

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January.

A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. This risks leaving the political initiative with the White House, and an increasingly hardline Iranian leadership.

articles.title: Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida
articles.summary: Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner to be preserved and turned into a museum, but it will now become the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

blocks.text: This archival video shows the SS United States in 2025 as it starts its move to Florida on its way to become the world's largest artificial reef.
A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.
Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.
Image source, Getty Images
Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.
A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.

The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A 2015 image from when the ship was docked in Philadelphia

blocks.text: A 2015 image from when the ship was docked in Philadelphia
Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.
Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.

blocks.caption: Image caption, SS United States in the 1950's

blocks.text: SS United States in the 1950's
Instead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.
The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.
Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on.
"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

articles.title: Missing 11-month-old baby found buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
articles.summary: Officials say the child was found close to his father's home on Tuesday, a day after he was taken, and is being cared for in hospital.

blocks.text: An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

Sharpe was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.
The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.
Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.
The search for Sharpe began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.
Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Sharpe.

Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Sharpe. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.
He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.

Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's father's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".
"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.
He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Sharpe to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.

"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.
Of the parents relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.

Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Sharpe's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.
"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

articles.title: TV providers say Rogers' Monday hockey move inflates prices, 'erodes' sports viewing
articles.summary: A trio of television providers are accusing Rogers Communications Inc. of violating competition rules and inflating Canadian sports fans' bills by moving Monday night hockey broadcasts exclusively to…

image.caption: In a letter submitted to Canada's broadcasting regulator on Tuesday, Cogeco Inc., Eastlink and SaskTel say Rogers is forcing price inflation on fans. (Cole Burston/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: NHL

A trio of television providers are accusing Rogers Communications Inc. of violating competition rules and inflating Canadian sports fans' bills by moving Monday night hockey broadcasts exclusively to its Sportsnet Plus streaming service for this NHL season.
Cogeco Inc., Eastlink and SaskTel say Rogers is forcing price inflation on fans
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 11, 2026 1:10 PM EST | Last Updated: 19 minutes ago

In a letter submitted to Canada's broadcasting regulator on Tuesday, the companies — Cogeco Inc., Eastlink and SaskTel — say Rogers is forcing price inflation on fans by charging a $12.99 monthly add-on fee to access hockey games on Monday nights, unless they already subscribe to Rogers TV or Sportsnet Plus.

The rival providers are asking the CRTC to order Rogers to immediately offer the content to independent companies for distribution to their customers for free, "ensuring parity" with Rogers' offering.

They say the dynamic is "deliberately degrading the user experience on other distributors' platforms" and leading to the "erosion of sports on television," as such companies are unable to assemble a comprehensible sports lineup for their own subscribers.

The shift of Monday broadcasts exclusively to Rogers' streaming platform is one of a few significant changes for hockey fans this season, which also includes the end of a sublicensing agreement that allowed Saturday night NHL broadcasts to air on CBC under the Hockey Night in Canada brand.

Rogers also upped the annual cost of Sportsnet Plus for premium subscribers to $344.99, and announced a 12-year agreement with Amazon for Prime Video in Canada to exclusively broadcast Wednesday night regular-season national games.
The ongoing 2026-27 NHL season marks the first under Rogers' 12-year, $11-billion national TV rights deal for English broadcasts.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sammy Hudes is a business reporter with The Canadian Press

articles.title: Integration of immigrants in Germany: Much has been accomplished but problems remain
articles.summary: Integration Report: While the integration of people with a migrant background is improving, violent youth remain a problem. This could soon spark political controversy.

image.caption: Nurses Lais Oliveira from Brazil and Thi Theu Nguyen from Vietnam are examples of successful immigrationImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Few topics in Germany spark as many heated debates as integration. How successful have efforts been to integrate new arrivals? What is needed to enable successful integration? And what are the biggest problems? Every two years, the government's Commissioner for Integration presents a comprehensive set of statistics on the matter. Since last year, that role has been held by Natalie Pawlik, a parliamentary representative from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Speaking in Berlin on Wednesday, Pawlik offered an overall positive assessment: "Integration is improving steadily, despite ongoing hurdles and challenges." She continued: "The people of our country want integration to succeed. They rightly expect that people who live in Germany permanently will learn our language and abide by our laws." The Commissioner for Integration is part of the Federal Ministry of Labor because ensuring that newcomers find work quickly is especially important.
Employment rate of immigrants in Germany higher than in most EU countries

Theintegration reportwas created by a team led by Frank Kalter, director of the German Center for Integration and Migration Research (DeZIM), drawing on official government statistics, surveys and independent studies. They found that when all immigrant groups are counted, about 30% of the population today has some sort of immigrant background — even if that means only one parent.

Pawlik commented: "This is an important message at a time when the discussion often focuses primarily on problems related to supposedly failed integration." Kalter also pointed out that the employment rate among immigrants in Germany is higher than in most other EU countries — nearly 70%.

And they work primarily in one sector: "In recent years, the biggest increase of workers without German citizenship has been in the health and social services sector." According to the data, there were about 1.8 million people without a German passport working in Germany in 2009. By 2025, this number had more than tripled to 5.8 million.
Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet
Concerns about unemployed mothers and violent youth

However, there are still plenty of problems. In nearly all immigrant groups, women have difficulty finding employment, especially if they have children and their husbands are employed. Only about 60% of women in such families are employed, whereas nearly 88% of women in families with German passports are employed.

There are also immigrant groups that face barriers to accessing educational opportunities and the job market: mostly young men who came to Germany as refugees. And if one considers only citizenship as a distinguishing factor, the percentage of convicted criminals who are not German citizens is far higher — at 40% — than their share of the population. And they are also reported to the police far more frequently. At the same time, individuals without a German passport are more likely to become victims themselves.
Germany relies on Syrian workers amid return debates
Government cuts funding for integration courses

Pawlik emphasizes that language acquisition is the foundation and starting point of any successful integration. But this is precisely where the government tightened its purse strings earlier this year in an effort to save money. Many integration courses are now no longer offered at all or receive less government funding. Pawlik made it clear that she is strongly critical of these cuts, even though she herself is part of the federal government.

Most recently, Pawlik and her fellow Social Democrats have been advocating for people who have been working in Germany for some time to receive more secure residency permits — especially those from Syria and Ukraine. On Tuesday, SPD lawmakers adopted a position paper on the matter. In the paper, they propose that existing legal rights that allow workers to remain in the country should also apply to refugees. In other words, it would give working refugees a more secure status.

But will the conservatives from the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union(CSU) — who lead the coalition led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) — support this? "You'll have to ask the interior minister," Pawlik replied when asked by DW. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) is known for being a hardliner on immigration policy.
This article was originally published in German.
