articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 42: Loose investment, conflict of interest raised
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s loose investment in GenCorp Industries Inc., which earned her P2.14 million in income despite not being listed as the firm"s shareholder in corporate records, took…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 10:42pm

Vice President Sara Duterte’s loose investment in GenCorp Industries Inc., which earned her P2.14 million in income despite not being listed as the firm’s shareholder in corporate records, took center stage during Day 42 of her impeachment trial.

Lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay, in-house counsel of GenCorp and Metro City Chow Foods Corp., testified that this loose interest stemmed from the investment she made in Davao Bounty Times Corporation, an entity that was supposed to operate the Jollibee Times Square branch in Davao City.
Punay, however, said the subject Jollibee branch was not granted a franchise and that it opened under Great Jolly Times Food Corp., which eventually became GenCorp.

Punay’s testimony, however, did not explain why GenCorp was paying out the Vice President for her return of capital worth over P2 million from 2022 to 2025 when her investment was made to Davao Bounty Times Corporation.
Impeachment court presiding officer Senator Francis Escudero told Punay they will issue a subpoena for additional documents that would justify the legality of GenCorp’s payout to the Vice President.

Ahead of disclosing Duterte's loose interest in GenCorp, Punay said that the Vice President is not a stockholder of the company, one of her declared business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
Punay said the Vice President’s name did not appear on the General Information Sheets (GIS) of GenCorp from 2022 to 2025.
Likewise, Punay said the Vice President did not receive dividends in those years since there were no dividends declared by the firm.
But upon further questioning of the senator-judges, she said that the P2.14 million was given to Duterte.
Senator-judge Francis Pangilinan said that Punay was wrong in saying that Duterte had no participation in GenCorp; being a recipient of a payout makes her a beneficiary.

During cross-examination of private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan, the defense witness also said that GenCorp has not issued an official or any public statement disputing Duterte's declaration that she is one of GenCorp’s stockholders.
Punay said it was not her responsibility to inform GenCorp about Duterte's SALN declarations identifying the company as one of her business interests, even after she assumed the vice presidency.

"I believe that my function as counsel of GenCorp [does not include] looking at other people's SALNs and adjusting our records just because somebody declared that he [or she] is a stockholder of our corporation," she said.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said an apparent conflict of interest situation has emerged from Punay’s testimony because GenCorp paid P2.14 million to Duterte and at the same time bagged P33 million worth of government contracts from the Davao City government led by the Vice President’s brother, Mayor Sebastian Duterte.
“So mukhang conflict of interest… Dahil sa kabilang banda, ‘yung investment binabayaran, ‘yung kita sa investment. Sa kabilang banda naman, nagbebenta ng pagkain sa Davao LGU,” he said.
(So it appears to be a conflict of interest because, on one hand, the returns on the investment are being paid, while on the other, the company is selling food to the Davao City government.)

Meanwhile, Punay also said that Duterte has no participation in Metro City Chow’s company affairs even if the company’s GIS from 2022 to 2025 lists her as a member of the Board of Directors and a member of the compensation committee.
“She did not participate…I have not seen her in the meetings, either board meetings or even company parties, even in the store, in the branch,” she said.
The witness also claimed that Duterte does not participate in the decision-making process, the operational management, or in the administration of the properties of the company. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Bataan Peninsula State Uni grad tops midwives licensure exam
articles.summary: A graduate of Bataan Peninsula State University achieved the highest score in the licensure examination for midwives held earlier this month.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 10:41pm
A graduate of Bataan Peninsula State University achieved the highest score in the licensure examination for midwives held earlier this month.

articles.title: COP31 leaders try out new sales pitch for climate action: Do it for the economy
articles.summary: John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, says he likes the reframing of the issue

blocks.text: FAMILY PHOTO. Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pose for a family photo with other leaders during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 11, 2026.
Murad Sezer/Reuters
John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, says he likes the reframing of the issue

items: Leaders at the COP31 summit are promoting climate action as a means to boost the economy and reduce living costs, addressing the urgent concerns of inflation and energy security.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres emphasized the vulnerability of countries dependent on fossil fuel imports and advocated for a transition to renewable energy to mitigate economic instability.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ANTALYA, Turkey – Leaders at the COP31 summit in Turkey are trying out a new sales pitch for climate action that is tailored to the times: do it to bolster the economy and bring down the cost of living.

The message, being repeated in the hallways and on the plenary stage of the annual UN conference, reflects efforts by organizers to capture the attention of governments wrestling with crises that have pushed global warming down the list of priorities.

Among those is rampant inflation driven in part by disruptions to Middle East crude oil shipments since the onset of the Iran war. Consumer price pressures from fuel to food were a major driver in the US midterm elections that handed control of Congress to Democrats, and are an important vulnerability for leaders across Europe, Asia and elsewhere.

“Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders attending the summit on Wednesday, November 11.
“Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown,” he added, saying the clear solution is a shift to renewable energy.

Simon Stiell, head of the UN’s climate office, made the same point. “Today, chaos in global energy markets and climate disasters are supercharging inflation, slamming government budgets, pushing household bills up and living standards down,” he told the conference.
“The political costs of fossil fuel dependency are unforgiving. Climate action can help relieve the pressures.”
John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, said he liked the reframing of the issue.

Climate change has become a massively divisive political issue in recent years, including in the US, where President Donald Trump last year withdrew the world’s top historical greenhouse gas emitter from international climate cooperation after calling warming a hoax.
“I think everybody who is working on climate needs to change the way they talk about it,” Kerry told reporters on the sidelines of the summit.
“I think that grouping of security, health, jobs, stability of communities and food supply are all very real and very much on people’s minds when I talk to them.”
European energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said the approach could help build a consensus for action that could even include climate skeptics.

“Because even if you don’t believe in climate change, which I obviously do, we should be able to agree that moving away from a dependency on fossils is extremely smart for security reasons,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Parts of B.C. could be without power for days as storm continues to batter province
articles.summary: B.C. Hydro is warning that some drenched areas of the province could be without power for days, as a fall storm continued to make its presence felt on Wednesday.

image.caption: A person walks their dog past Vancouver's Coal Harbour last Friday. A number of areas that lost power over the weekend could be without power for a while longer, as a parade of storms continues to affect the province. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
B.C. Hydro is warning that some drenched areas of the province could be without power for days, as a fall storm continued to make its presence felt on Wednesday.
Rainfall expected to intensify on Wednesday for west and inland Vancouver Island, forecasters say

Some areas of British Columbia have been without power since late last week after a series of storms rolled through, with more than 400,000 customers in total left without power between Friday and Monday, according to B.C. Hydro.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) has maintained a number of rainfall and wind warnings throughout B.C. on Wednesday, saying more than 250 millimetres of rain is possible for parts of western and inland Vancouver Island.
Flood watches are also in place throughout southwest B.C., as officials warn drivers to be prepared for pooling water and debris on the South Coast after the storm made landfall on Tuesday.

items: More than 250 mm of rain forecast for parts of B.C. as storm makes landfall
Zeballos evacuation orders to remain in place for days after landslide

blocks.text: In an update on Tuesday night, B.C. Hydro said that restoring power after the parade of storms has proven challenging due to the extensive repairs required.
"Access remains challenging in some areas due to fallen trees, debris and soft ground conditions," the utility said.

The #BC River Forecast Centre has issued a High Streamflow Advisory for the Fraser Valley including areas around #Chilliwack and #HopeBC, the Fraser Canyon and #Chilcotin. Stay away from fast-flowing rivers & potentially unstable riverbanks. More info: https://t.co/W87tVOtUlp #BCFlood—EmergencyInfoBC
The village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island, where an evacuation order was issued last week due to a landslide, will likely remain without power for a few more days yet, it said.

"Specialized equipment is required and must be transported by helicopter due to the remote location and challenging terrain," the B.C. Hydro update reads. "The earliest crews can access the site is Thursday, provided weather conditions allow safe access."
Warning for drivers

The weather warnings posted throughout B.C. cover the entirety of Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii, as well as the Sunshine Coast, the central Interior and Prince George areas, and portions of Metro Vancouver and the Fraser Canyon.

In west and inland Vancouver Island, ECCC says that rainfall rates could go as high as 20 millimetres per hour at times on Wednesday, and up to 160 millimetres of rain could fall on the Sea-to-Sky Highway by Thursday morning.
"Localized flooding is likely. Some roads may become impassable," the warning reads.

The Ministry of Transportation and Transit has issued a Traffic Advisory for the South Coast region, including the Lower Mainland, #SunshineCoast, #VancouverIsland & the Fraser Valley. Drivers should prepare for winds, heavy rainfall & possible flooding. Never drive across flooded roads, bridges or river crossings. Follow @DriveBC for updates. More info: https://t.co/sHy7chVK6E #BCStorm #BCFlood #BC—EmergencyInfoBC
B.C.'s Ministry of Transportation issued a traffic advisory on Tuesday, warning commuters on the South Coast to be prepared and check DriveBC before heading out.

Areas that could be most affected, according to the ministry's traffic advisory, are the Sea-to-Sky Highway, Highway 1 through the Fraser Valley and Fraser Canyon, and the Malahat and western coast communities on Vancouver Island.

articles.title: DSWD: More than 1,300 vendors affected by ASEAN Summit
articles.summary: The vendors whose livelihoods have been disrupted are receiving cash aid and family food packs from the Department of Social Welfare and Development

blocks.text: AYUDA. Vendors in Pasay City affected by the ASEAN Summit receive P10,000 from the Department of Social Welfare and Development on November 11, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
The vendors whose livelihoods have been disrupted are receiving cash aid and family food packs from the Department of Social Welfare and Development

MANILA, Philippines – There are more than 1,300 vendors whose livelihoods have been affected by the Philippines’ hosting of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits, according to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said on Wednesday, November 11, that the Parañaque City government forwarded to the DSWD a list of vendors affected in Baclaran, a bustling market area, amid security measures implemented for the event.

The city government said street vendors are “temporarily prohibited” from operating along Roxas Boulevard and its service roads, from Redemptorist Road to Quirino Avenue, as well as the road beneath the Light Rail Transit (LRT) until November 20.

blocks.caption: Parañaque clears Baclaran roads of street vendors for ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: Since Baclaran is near Pasay City as well, the DSWD is also coordinating with the local government to identify more affected vendors in the area.

“Bagamat humihingi kami ng paumanhin sa mga naantala ang hanapbuhay dahil sa napipintong ASEAN Summit, ang direktiba ng ating Pangulo ay masigurado na mabigyan sila ng tulong pinansyal kasi alam natin na wala silang kikitain sa mga araw na ‘yon,” Gatchalian said on the sidelines of cash aid distribution in Pasay City.

(We apologize to those whose livelihoods were put on hold because of the upcoming ASEAN Summit, but the directive of the President is to ensure that they will be given financial support because we know they will not have earnings during those days.)

blocks.caption: DSWD: More than 1,300 vendors affected by ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: In Pasay City, around 50 ambulant vendors and eatery workers received P10,000 from the DSWD’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program on Wednesday. They were also given family food packs.
It was the second batch following the aid distribution to some 30 individuals on Sunday, November 8.
Most of the beneficiaries were located along Diokno Boulevard.

“Malaking tulong na rin naman po kahit papaano…. Pagkakasyahin hangga’t walang trabaho (This is still a great help somehow. We’ll make do with it while we have no work),” said Anabel de Luna, 34. The eatery where she works temporarily closed on Monday, November 9, and may resume operations on November 20 or 21.
But others like Rizal Villaula, a 40-year-old pares cart owner, had to stop selling on October 22 amid road clearing operations. He has since entered into multiple gigs, like towing services.
Maria Joanna Cristina Samarro, a 46-year-old ambulant vendor, has been selling cigarettes for the past weeks to earn just enough for some meals.

But she took the chance to set up her table in front of the Senate building, also along Diokno Boulevard, to sell various items such as bread, coffee, and soft drinks, as protesters gathered there on Wednesday morning.
When there are no road restrictions, she can earn up to P500 a day.
Gatchalian said affected vendors in Parañaque City will receive their cash aid and food packs by Thursday, November 12.
Malacañang earlier declared November 16 to 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila to make way for the ASEAN Summit. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
articles.summary: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
articles.byline: Nick Beake, Guy Hedgecoe, Alba Morgade

blocks.text: Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.
Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056).
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.
Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.
Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.
"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."
He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."
With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".
However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.
"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.
Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.
Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

articles.title: Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador
articles.summary:
Tomás Beltrán was shot dead amid gang warfare that has turned Latin American country into one of its most violent

Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when…

blocks.text: Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.

Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.

Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.

Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.

“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.

“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.

The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.

“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.

Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.

While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.

There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

articles.title: Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years in protest at rising housing costs
articles.summary:
The 24-hour stoppage has drawn high participation across sectors and comes weeks before election in which far right could gain power

Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s…
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid and Stephen Burgen in Barcelona

blocks.text: Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly backed by the country’s largest unions as well as tenants’ associations, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis.

Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.”

While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalusia, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute.

Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to an ongoing strike by teachers that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. In Madrid, scuffles broke out between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while demonstrators dragged ⁠large recycling bins on to the streets to block traffic. By midday on Wednesday, government officials said 27 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country.

blocks.caption: Protesters set fire to tyres at a roadblock on Wednesday in Barcelona. Photograph: Andreu Dalmau/EPA

blocks.text: Stormy weather loomed over the plans for afternoon marches across the country after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, rough seas and heavy rains.

The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades.

As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties were increasingly being used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.

Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristed areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable.

blocks.caption: An estate agents’ office in Móstoles, Madrid, covered with stickers calling on people to join the general strike. Photograph: Angel Perez/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as limits on the evictions of vulnerable people, rent freezes and a crackdown on short-term rentals.
Unai Sordo, the head of one of the country’s biggest labour unions, the Workers’ Commissions, told Cadena Ser radio: “There is one issue that is dividing the country: the struggle to access housing.”

Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis.
after newsletter promotion
Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year.

This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour workday and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said.

blocks.caption: Teachers protest at a metro station in Madrid on Wednesday. Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPA

blocks.text: His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, said unions were trying to help Sánchez remain in office.

This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.”

While she acknowledged that union activity is a constitutional right, she also said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”

articles.title: Italy: Hundreds of schools evacuated after bomb threats
articles.summary: Although the government believes the threat to be a hoax, it has nevertheless prompted concerns about "hybrid warfare" in Europe. Similar messages were sent in Northern Ireland, Ireland, and Bulgaria.

image.caption: Police arrived at schools in Milan and other cities in ItalyImage: Luca Bruno/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: At 10 a.m. local time on Wednesday, 312 Italian schools received the same e-mail: "A powerful explosive device with a remote detonator has been left in your building."
Most of the affected schools were in Rome, but several other major cities also got the same message.
Antonello Giannelli, head of the National Association of School Principals, said that it was "clearly the work of a hoaxer" trying to sow chaos.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said it was also designed to "sow terror" for thousands of families.

blocks.caption: Schools in Naples were also among those affectedImage: Sergio Siano/IPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet will convene an emergency meeting this afternoon, the Palazzo Chigi has confirmed.
"The government is closely monitoring the numerous reports of bomb threats at schools," Meloni said in a statement posted to social media.
"Law enforcement agencies and government institutions at every level are working to monitor the situation and reassure citizens, families, and school staff.
"At this time, based on the investigations conducted, there is no evidence to suggest that a concrete danger exists. Rather, the reports appear to be part of a strategy aimed at causing alarm."
Concerns over hybrid warfare
The threatening e-mail sent to Italian schools was signed with the same fake name as similar messages that went out to newsrooms in Bulgaria and Ireland on Friday.
Some 300 schools in Northern Ireland were also affected, though it was immediately clear if the threats had come from the same sender.

Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries amongst leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

Crosetto also cautioned against jumping to conclusions, saying: "It is not always ​the work of foreign countries or hostile entities. There are also attention-seekers and lunatics who" simply want to unleash mayhem.

articles.title: Tundu Lissu: After escaping the death penalty, what does his guilty verdict mean for Tanzania's democracy?
articles.summary: A treason trial could have meant death by hanging for Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu. Instead, he now faces four years in prison for incitement to unrest. Ban dissident voices truly be heard…
articles.byline: Eddy Micah Jr., Imani Henrick Luvanga, Isaac Mugabi, Benita van Eyssen

image.caption: Opposition figure Tundu Lissu originally faced the death penalty for treasonImage: ChademaTZ2/X

blocks.text: On November 6, Tundu Lissu, leader of Tanzania's main opposition Chadema party, was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections.
The same day, he was cleared of treason charges — which could have meant a death sentence if he had been found guilty.

Lissu commented that the judiciary had acted under pressure; he rejected the verdict due to the fact that incitement was not among the charges which had brought against him at the start of his trial in 2025.
Chadema officials have now signaled an intention to appeal the court decision. The government has not issued a statement on his conviction yet.

blocks.caption: Police officers also detained several of Lissu's supporters during clashes in April 2025Image: Emmanuel Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tanzania's most dramatic trial in decades

Few opposition figures have shaped modern Tanzanian politics as dramatically as Lissu. A lawyer by training and one of the country's most outspoken critics of the ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), Lissu has spent years challenging the political establishment.

Over the years, he has been subjected to repeated arrest and detention; in 2017, he survived an attempt on his life by unknown gunmen outside his residence in the capital Dodoma, sustaining multiple bullet wounds.

More recently, his trial in the run-up to the October 2025 general election continued to keep him and the opposition in the public eye following his arrest in April 2025 in the southwestern town of Mbinga.
Why was Tundu Lissu arrested?
Prosecuters accused Lissu of encouraging the public to prevent the 2025 election from taking place and charged him with one count of treason.
As legal evidence, they cited social media posts he had made, in which he was seen to be calling on Tanzanians to boycott the vote over concerns about possible electoral malpractice.
In the end, the election went ahead without Chadema on October 29, which was marred by violence on an unprecedented in scale in Tanzania; security forces even used live ammunition on protesters.

Francis Ibrahim, an independent political analyst based in Dar es Salaam, told DW that "heads have to roll from the law enforcement side, who overstretched their mandate, all the way to the people, who financed, planned and organized [this crackdown]."
But after a nationwide internet shutdown and curfew following the election violence, incumbent President Samia Suluhu Hassan was named winner with 98% of the vote.
Tanzania's post-election violence: No justice after a year
What does the verdict mean for democracy?
Ibrahim believes that the removal of the capital treason charge could be interpreted as a move towards rapprochment with voters.
"What I can tell you is that they are looking for a political deescalation that could solve the crisis," he explained, adding that Lissu might yet get to have a small say in politics after all:

"There has to be a process of [creating] a new constitution, and it needs everybody on the table," he said, adding that Lissu might therefore perhaps be released early in order to partake in discussions and negotiations.

However when in late July, President Suluhu Hassan met with representatives of more than a dozen political parties to discuss national reconciliation and constitutional reform, Chadema officials were explicitly not party to the consultations.
German lawmakers press Tanzania over rights concerns
Politics at play behind the verdict?
Public opinion meanwhile varies on Lissu's verdict, with many Tanzanians however saying that the trial was politically motivated in their view.
Ruqaya Mohammed, the National Deputy Secretary of the oppsition ACT-Wazalendo party's youth wing, told DW, "ee are getting into a darker space in our political arena."
"I think it's the right time now, as a nation, to have open dialogue on some reforms, on the legal perspective and electoral reforms. Maybe if we manage ... that, we can see a light," she explained.

blocks.caption: Security forces were deployed during the Tundu Lissu trial in Dar es Salaam, with the mandate to ensure public orderImage: Emmanuel Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Most others, however, remain reluctant to go on record for fear of reprisal; a musician and human rights advocate was among few who agreed to speak to DW — on the strict condition of anonymity.

In his view, Tanzanians simply are not free to express themselves publicly at all: "You saw the terror atmosphere and climate of fear outside the court premises when Tundu's judgement was ... read. Such is the broader display of what Tanzania looks like," he told DW.

"Opposition politics has been suppressed for years, and his conviction is just a continuation of what has been happening. It's a miracle that he is still alive. To put him in jail from four years is far from the worst-case scenario."
Youth turn to digital activism as Tanzania clamps down
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

articles.title: PH to get coastal radar, surveillance drones from Japan under P1.7-B security deal
articles.summary: Japan has committed 4.3 billion yen (approximately P1.7 billion) in security assistance to the Philippines, including the provision of a coastal radar system for the Philippine Navy and unmanned…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 9:28pm

Japan has committed 4.3 billion yen (approximately P1.7 billion) in security assistance to the Philippines, including the provision of a coastal radar system for the Philippine Navy and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for the Philippine Air Force.

The agreement was formalized on Monday, November 9, through the signing and exchange of notes between Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Katsuro Kitagawa and Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro in Manila.
According to Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the assistance is part of its Fiscal Year 2026 Official Security Assistance (OSA) program.

The project marks the first transfer of defense equipment to the Philippines under Japan's OSA framework, which provides equipment, supplies, and infrastructure assistance to strengthen the security and defense capabilities of partner countries.
Under the agreement, the Philippine Navy will receive a coastal radar system, while the Philippine Air Force will be provided with UAVs for monitoring and surveillance operations.
The assistance is expected to strengthen the Armed Forces of the Philippines' maritime domain awareness and surveillance capabilities, particularly in monitoring strategic maritime areas.

Japan noted that the Philippines occupies a strategically important position along major sea lanes, including the South China Sea and the Luzon Strait, making the country an important partner in maintaining regional security.

The Japanese government also emphasized that the assistance would further strengthen security cooperation between the two countries, protect important maritime routes, and contribute to regional peace and stability.

Manila and Tokyo have continued to deepen their defense and security partnership as both countries work toward advancing a rules-based international order and a Free and Open Indo-Pacific. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: The remarkable story behind the secret Canadian guerilla force you've never heard of

image.caption: Some of the first soldiers of Force 136 during training in India in 1945. The covert Chinese Canadian force fought during the Second World War. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)

blocks.text: Brent G. Hoy's father, Charles Hoy, didn't talk much about what he did during the Second World War.
It wasn't just that it was difficult. He also was part of a covert Chinese Canadian force, sworn to secrecy.
Force 136, part of Britain's Special Operations Executive, was trained in espionage, guerilla warfare and jungle survival for parachute deployment behind enemy lines in Southeast Asia.
These soldiers wore a Canadian uniform and were prepared to sacrifice their lives, despite being shunned by their country, both in law and daily discrimination.
"Fighting for a country that really didn't want you, but nevertheless having that deep sense to contribute," Hoy said of his father.
That complicated legacy is being spotlighted in a black and white photograph selected by Canada Post for a new stamp, to commemorate the country's military history.

It shows 10 out of about 150 Chinese Canadian soldiers who served the Allied war effort with Force 136 and, after the war was won in 1945, came home to become part of a broader push to change how their community was treated. In 1947, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed and the entrenched racism Chinese Canadians experienced began to shift.
It was a double victory, says Catherine Clement, a historian and curator whose work excavates stories of the Chinese Canadian experience.
"Helping the Allies win the war, but also helping the Chinese community to win the right, like equal rights, full rights of citizens of Canada".
Canada Post's new Remembrance Day stamp shows 10 soldiers from Force 136 awaiting repatriation in 1945. Brent G. Hoy's father, Charles Hoy, is in the bottom row, second from the right. (Canada Post)

Between 1885 and 1923, Chinese immigrants who came to Canada had to pay at least $50 to enter. The head tax was later raised to $100, then $500, before all Chinese immigration was banned in July 1923.

From then until 1947, all Chinese people — even those born in Canada — were required to register with the government or risk fines, detainment or deportation. They were segregated within society too, like being prevented from working in some professions or swimming in some public pools.
Operation Oblivion
It was under those laws, designed to exclude or ostracize people on the basis of their Chinese ethnicity, that Hoy's father, at the age of 26, still decided to volunteer in the war effort for Canada.

It was the same story for Rick Wong's father, Hank Wong, the son of a head tax payer and a member of Force 136, also called Operation Oblivion. Hank, who died in 2019, was the last surviving member of the original 13 members of the top secret mission to sabotage supply lines and equipment within Japanese-occupied territory in the Pacific.

Wong says despite first being rejected from the navy, because it was "for white men only," his father eventually joined the Kent Regiment and learned to parachute out of planes and rapidly deploy from moving trucks.

It was in the 1940s, when Japan entered the Second War War and began to quickly invade and occupy large parts of Southeast Asia, that the British realised it needed agents in the region to support local resistance fighters.
Undercover resistance
An undated photo of the first recruits of Force 136 training in Darwin, Australia. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)
Chinese Canadians were the perfect recruits, from the perspective of Britain's Special Operations Executive, easily blending in with local populations with language skills in English and Cantonese.
Force 136 was born.

Then began intense training in Canada and abroad, including in espionage, wireless operation and jungle survival. Their mission was to gather intelligence, support local resistance fighters and carry out sabotage operations.
They were told to expect extreme heat, insects and disease, alongside the dangers of capture, torture or death.
Members of Force 136 training in Queensland, Australia in 1945. (Chinese Canadian Military Museum)
'A suicide mission'
One recruit, dropped into Borneo, recalled living on crocodile meat, monkeys and wild pigs, in a story highlighted by the Chinese Canadian Military Museum.
"They were told to save your last bullet for yourself, carry cyanide, if you're captured don't reveal any secrets," said Wong.
He says he once asked his father if he was afraid about what was "essentially a suicide mission" while he was awaiting his deployment in Australia.
His father replied, "you gotta do what you gotta do."

Then the Americans dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, in early August 1945. More than 80,000 people were killed instantly. A few days later, the war ended and so too did Operation Oblivion.
While most of Force 136 sailed back to Canada through England, some men, including Wong's father, were abandoned in Australia.
"They had to work their way back on a freighter in order to get back," said Wong.

When they did get back to Canada, it took another two years until discriminatory laws were repealed. Many see Force 136 and the dismembering of legislation like the Chinese Exclusion Act as inseparably linked.

When those men returned they continued fighting, says Melissa Karmen Lee, the CEO of the Chinese Canadian Museum in Vancouver. It's the only place in Canada, including the War Museum in Ottawa, where the public can see a permanent exhibit on Chinese Canadian soldiers.
"Their faces belong on a Canadian stamp, their stories belong in our history books, and their legacy belongs to every Canadian," Lee said.
Rick Wong, left, and Brent G. Hoy unveil the new Canada Post stamp in Vancouver on Nov. 3. (Spill Studios)
'That's my dad there'

Hoy told an audience at the unveiling of the stamp in Vancouver that he could visualize his father's "broad and knowing closed lip smile of approval" that the contributions of Force 136 would be memorialized in such a way.
His father, who died in 2002, appears in the stamp in the bottom row, second from the right.
Hoy says he was thrilled "beyond words" when he was sent a mock-up of the stamp.
"I thought, hey gee, you know that's my dad there."

While the stamp features only a handful of the faces behind Force 136, Hoy says it marks an acknowledgement of gratitude for the Chinese Canadians that were prepared to sacrifice their lives. None lived long enough to see this commemoration.
"This selfless sense of duty shines a bright light on the fact that we, as a generation after them, are the offspring of our ancestors' courage, persistence, commitment and sacrifice."

articles.title: Sara Duterte’s ‘loose investments’ in Gencorp earn her P2.1-M ‘return of capital’
articles.summary: An article of incorporation presented by the prosecution during the impeachment trial shows the Vice President paid P46,000 in capital stock

blocks.text: An article of incorporation presented by the prosecution during the impeachment trial shows the Vice President paid P46,000 in capital stock

MANILA, Philippines – An in-house corporate counsel of Gencorp Industries Inc. denied that Vice President Sara Duterte has business interests in the company, despite it being listed in her sworn Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs).

On Day 42 of the impeachment trial on Wednesday, November 11, Suzette Balucanag-Punay refuted a portion of the forensic financial report of lawyer Alexander Cabrera, which indicated that Duterte owns a 20% stake in Gencorp and has paid-up capital in the company amounting to P250,000.

Balucanag-Punay also said Duterte is not a stockholder of Gencorp and does not participate in any stockholders’ meetings. She said the Vice President also has no involvement in the board of directors, management, as well as in the decision-making of the company.
“She is not a beneficial owner of Gencorp,” the corporate counsel told the impeachment court.
Balucanag-Punay, however, said Duterte received more than P2.1 million in “return of capital” from Gencorp between 2022 and 2025 from what she described as “loose investment.”
Duterte received return of capital amounting to P337,500 from Gencorp in 2022; P555,750 from May to December 2023; P612,419 in 2024; and P636,700 in 2025.
She, however, did not receive any return of capital from January to April 2023.

“I termed it as a loose investment, your honor. It’s coming from the contributions that the Vice President made for Davao Bounty Times before the actual commencement of the operations of Jollibee Times Square,” said Balucanag-Punay.

According to the witness, Duterte initially invested in Davao Bounty Foods Corporation, a company that attempted to acquire the franchise of a Jollibee branch in Davao. The franchise, however, was not granted, and Duterte’s investments were carried over to the companies that operated the Jollibee Times Square branch, including Gencorp.
Gencorp now operates five Jollibee branches in Davao: Centerpoint Plaza, Davao Gaisano Mall, Abreeza Mall, Times Square Plaza Center, and Bolton.
Balucanag-Punay said Duterte’s investments only covered the Jollibee Times Square branch and not Gencorp. She also said she is unaware of the nature of the investments and their exact amount.
An article of incorporation presented by the prosecution showed Duterte paid capital stock to Davao Bounty amounting to P46,000.
Prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan pressed Balucanag-Punay on Duterte’s possible other investments in Gencorp, citing the ballooning of her investment from P46,000 to P2.14 million.

“I am unaware if there’s any because I cannot verify it from other records,” Balucanag-Punay said, adding she could not confirm how the returns of capital were calculated and if the Vice President still receives income from Gencorp.

Article XII, Section VII of the 1987 Constitution prohibits the president, vice president, and members of the Cabinet from holding any other office or employment during their tenure. They are also barred from “directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries.”
Balucanag-Punay’s responses did not sit well with some senator-judges, including Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo, who questioned her credibility.
“You know that you will testify here, so you should have researched. Now, you cannot even present any document that would back up your claims that it was return of investment,” Tulfo said.
Duterte is facing impeachment proceedings under Article II of the articles of impeachment, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth, including allegedly undeclared assets and properties.
As part of the impeachment article, the prosecution challenged Duterte’s inclusion of stock ownership in Gencorp in her 2024-2025 SALN, despite her name’s absence on the company’s corporate records.

In a related development, the defense dropped some of its witnesses, announcing they were dispensing with the testimonies of subpoenaed bank officials — except representatives from Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) — to expedite the proceedings.

“We don’t think there’s a need to waste the time of the court in presenting all of the bank representatives, so we tightened the list and left only the BPI official. It’s in the interest of expediting the proceedings,” defense lawyer Michael Poa said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
articles.summary: The country begins a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, provided no new cases are recorded.

blocks.text: Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.

Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.

The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.

Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June.
But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE.
The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures.
Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

articles.title: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
articles.summary: Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah is being tried on the charge of "publishing false news" and potentially faces imprisonment.

blocks.text: A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation.
Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge.
The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists".
Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left".
She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next."
Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.

Last month, another Cairo court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down.

After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge.

Egypt has largely stifled freedom of the press, ranking 169th out of 180 countries for press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders' 2026 analysis. The group says that at least 26 journalists who were arrested in recent years remain in detention.

While most newspapers and television stations now keep to government lines, Mada Masr remained a rare, independent and investigative news source in Egypt. However, since 2017 the site could only be viewed from outside the country.
It had reported on alleged corruption and human rights abuses, and provided deep coverage of politics and economics, as well as regional upheaval and wars in Libya, Sudan and Gaza.

In her BBC interview on Sunday, Attalah insisted that the factual reporting and professional standards of Mada Masr had an important role to play in Egyptian society, which could benefit the government.

"It's much better if you have a little space left to have it open for professional media organisations who do rigorous reporting, because if we disappear, then you make the space for conspiracies and disinformation," she said.
"People need to know, people need to consume information and you're shooting yourself in the foot if you're killing the newsrooms that do it properly."

In September, six journalists with the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh - constituting its entire newsroom - were arrested in home raids by the Egyptian authorities and held incommunicado for nearly a week.

They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism, and their lawyers report that several were beaten and electrocuted in detention. They say that no evidence has been presented linking them to the Brotherhood.

Egypt's former president Mohammed Morsi – who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood – was removed from power by the military, led by Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, in July 2013 after widespread protests. Under Sisi, who became president the following year, the Islamist movement was classed as a terrorist organisation, leading to a widespread clampdown.
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Thameen Al-Kheetan, called for the Matsda2sh reporters to be released, with all charges dropped.
He also said the case against Attalah "raises fresh concerns regarding due process and fair trial".
"We call on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information," Al-Kheetan said.

"The steps taken to suppress the continued work of both Matsda2sh and Mada Masr must be overturned. The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern."
Attalah has suggested the authorities might again be trying to silence independent voices at a time of economic strain in Egypt and regional instability.

It has been widely noted that recent legal action against journalists comes after the US State Department waived human rights conditions on $320m (£240m) in its foreign military funding for Egypt in September. This allowed the funds to be released as part of Washington's annual $1.3bn military aid package.

The BBC asked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio whether he had raised the recent crackdown on independent journalism with Egypt's Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, at their meeting about regional tensions in Paris on Monday.

"We didn't discuss it today," Rubio said. "But… like anything else in foreign policy, there's always a balancing act to further the national interest of the United States. And in the end, Egypt has been a reliable and good defence partner of the United States."
"That doesn't mean you agree with everything another government does," he went on, adding that he was not "opining about their journalists".

articles.title: Hundreds of Italian schools hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
articles.summary: Emails containing the false warnings were sent to schools in Rome, Naples, Vicenza, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and other Italian cities, officials say.

blocks.text: Some 300 schools across Italy have received bomb threats, according to Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara, who described the incidents as probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk".
Valditara told Italian TV that there was a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in Italy and elsewhere in Europe which had targeted flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.
The emails were sent to schools in Rome, Naples, Vicenza, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and many other Italian cities, and a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has called a meeting of top ministers and intelligence chiefs.
Meloni said the government was monitoring closely the "numerous reports of bomb threats at educational institutions" although checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Italian reports said 280 school head teachers had received threats in recent days.
Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, according to reports from a number of regions, and pupils were allowed to return to class.

In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

In a separate incident, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland were sent emails which police said they were treating as a hoax. Messages sent to number of schools in Scotland were also being treated by police as a hoax. It is unclear whether any of the incidents are connected.

articles.title: Transport workers in Chile block highways in protest over surging fuel prices
articles.summary: Hundreds of bus and lorry drivers are blocking traffic along major highway routes across the country.

blocks.text: Hundreds of transport workers in Chile have blocked roads and highways across the country in protest over high fuel prices.
Drivers of busses and lorries began protesting on Tuesday, gathering in convoys to halt traffic along major routes.
They are demanding a relief from surging diesel prices, which have been driven up by the war in Iran.
Talks between government officials and protest leaders have so far failed to reach a resolution, with another meeting expected to take place on Wednesday.
The protest is being organised by the ⁠Fuerza del Norte trade union, which represents around 80% of Chile's lorry drivers, and the No+TAG civic protest ​movement.

"There is no point of agreement with the government that could offer any perspective to find solutions for everyone," Andrés Alarcón, a spokesman for No+TAG, said after talks broke down on Tuesday, adding "the strike continues".
Economy Minister Daniel Mas called for further dialogue, but warned "at some point, we will have to clear the highways".
He stressed the protests were impacting economic activity and exports, saying "we need to get the country moving again".
The government of President José Antonio Kast has faced public discontent over fuel prices for months.
The average price of diesel has risen 74% since March, according to industry groups.
Juan Cornejo, the president of the Association of Intercity Bus Owners, which represents 14 mid-sized companies, told AFP that "we've reached our limit".
"We've spent more than a month working with negative numbers," he added.
Lorry driver Claudio Elguezabal, who took part in a protest near the capital, Santiago, on Tuesday morning, said the situation was unsustainable.
"Right now I'm not making any profit. Sometimes you even have to put in your own money to cover the client," AFP quoted the 47-year-old as saying.

articles.title: Germany news: Only 1/3 of Germans satisfied with state of democracy
articles.summary: A new authoritarianism study has revealed a new low in satisfaction levels with the functioning of German democracy. Meanwhile, the Bundeswehr has banned Chinese-made drones. DW has more.

image.caption: The study also found a high level of chauvinistic and antisemitic tendencies among respondentsImage: James Zabel/Kirchner-Media/IMAGO

blocks.text: November 11, 2026
Satisfaction with democracy in Germany reaches new low — study
Just a third of respondents said they were satisfied with the state of democracy in the Federal Republic of Germany, according to a new report from the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study.

This marked a steep decline from the 42.3% level of satisfaction measured in the last study in 2024 and was the lowest point since the study began in 2002. The level was even lower in the former East German states where only 22.8% expressed satisfaction with German democracy, down from 29.7%.
At the same time, 89.3% of respondents said they agreed with the concept of democracy, however, this also marked the first time this level fell below 90%.
A large share of respondents also expressed chauvinistic and antisemitic views.
In response to the statement "Germany is being dangerously overrun by foreigners," 34.9% were manifestly in agreement, with 24.4% in latent agreement.
At the same time, 15.5% manifestly agreed with the statement "the influence of Jews in Germany is still too great," with 21.7% latently agreeing.
The research was carried out by the Else-Frenkel-Brunswik-Institut at the University of Leipzig. They surveyed 2,500 people between mid-March and the beginning of June this year.

articles.title: Iran classes Argentina navy, air force as 'terrorist organizations'
articles.summary: In a tit-for-tat move, Iran has said it now considers Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." Tehran claimed Buenos Aires is responsible for further consequences.

image.caption: Tehran did not mention Argentina's army in the statement [FILE: Mar 19, 2024]Image: Str/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that it classified Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations."

In early April, Argentina designated Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a "terrorist organization," as US President Donald Trump pressured his allies to do so following the war on Iran.
Tehran's designation came "based on the principle of reciprocity," Iran's ​Foreign ‌Ministry said in a statement.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival
"It is ‌evident ​that the responsibility for all consequences arising from this matter will lie with the Argentine government," the ministry added, ​without a mention of Argentina's army.
Iran passed a legislation in 2019 that grants retaliatory measures against states that designate its military as a terrorist group.
Argentina holds Hezbollah responsible for deadly attacks
Argentina said in April that it had taken action against the IRGC because of its support for the Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah.

blocks.caption: The 1994 bombing attack that destroyed the AMIA building in Buenos Aires left 85 people deadImage: Daniel Luna/dpa/picture-alliance

blocks.text: Buenos Aires holds Hezbollah responsible for the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center, which killed 85 people.
IRGC classified as a terrorist group by many countries
IRGC was established at the end of Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution as an elite armed militia whose role was to protect the then embryonic Shiite clerical regime.
Over the years, it has morphed into a vast economic and political empire. Rather than the elected president, the force answers directly to Iran's supreme leader.
The United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom, along with other countries, classify the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organization.

articles.title: GOP branded ‘sinking ship’ as Republicans block efforts to impeach Hegseth – US politics live
articles.summary: Trump hails ‘exoneration of a Great American Patriot’ as moves against his defense secretary fail for now

blocks.text: Key events

items: 15m agoGOP branded 'sinking ship' as House Republicans block efforts to impeach Hegseth

blocks.text: GOP branded 'sinking ship' as House Republicans block efforts to impeach Hegseth
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Republican representative Thomas Massie compared the GOP with passengers content to go down with the Titanic after colleagues thwarted his effort to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

The vote came a week after Republicans lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives in their worst midterm election in more than a half century, and underscored how lawmakers remain wary of crossing Donald Trump, who has signaled his continued support for Hegseth.
“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” Massie, a Republican congressman who lost his primary after breaking with the president, said.

Top Democrats announced their support for the resolution, but Republicans moved to kill it by referring it to the judiciary committee. Their motion succeeded on Tuesday, by a 211-204 vote, largely along party lines. Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the motion, along with all Democrats.
Trump, who was twice impeached, celebrated what he hailed as the “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot” and lashed out at Massie for forcing the vote.
“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump said on Truth Social. “They must be stopped!”

The Pentagon, meanwhile, declared “total victory”. “The referral of these baseless impeachment articles to the House judiciary committee marks total victory for Secretary Hegseth, the Department of War, and the American warfighter,” Sean Parnell, a department spokesperson, wrote in a social media post.
Some 11 Democratic representatives skipped the vote, the Daily Beast reported earlier this morning, causing the articles of impeachment to fail. Among those to miss the vote was Nancy Pelosi.
If eight of ‌them had voted with fellow Democrats the measure could have proceeded.

House Democratic leader Hakeen Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next ​Congress in January when the Democrats who triumphed in the midterm take their seats. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.
Read the full story here:
In other developments:

items: Congressman Jim Jordan, a Republican hardliner from Ohio, won the election to become the next House minority leader in Congress. Jordan beat Representative Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, by 106-73 in a closed-door vote to lead Republicans from January. He replaces the current House speaker, Mike Jonson, who said he would not run when the GOP cedes control to Democrats in the new year.

Meanwhile, Republicans in the upper chamber, re-elected John Thune to serve as Senate minority leader in the next Congress. The GOP senator from North Dakota didn’t face a challenger in the closed-door vote, as Democrats prepare for at least a 10-seat majority in the new year.

Nine members of the Kennedy family sued the Trump administration in an effort to block its construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch. The family’s complaint states that the arch, which is planned for near Arlington national cemetery, would obstruct the Kennedy gravesites, the JFK Eternal Flame and the sightlines of the cemetery, “permanently diminishing these memorials.”

A federal judge has allowed Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed. Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for $10bn over an edited clip that made it appear that Trump told his supporters to storm the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.
